title: Gradient Similarity Surgery in Multi-Task Deep Learning
venue: Proceedings of the European Conference on Machine Learning and Principles and Practice of Knowledge Discovery in Databases (ECML PKDD 2025)
role_in_thesis: Advances gradient surgery through SAM-GS by utilizing gradient magnitude similarity to equalize conflicting gradients and regulate first-order momentum during joint optimization.
problem: In multi-task deep learning, task gradients can conflict in direction or magnitude, and simple averaging lets dominant gradients steer updates, which degrades convergence of the task losses.
proposed_solution: The authors propose SAM-GS, a gradient surgery optimiser that measures task gradient magnitude similarity to trigger gradient equalisation on conflict and to modulate the first-order momentum otherwise.
claim: SAM-GS outperforms previous multi-task optimisation methods on two synthetic problems and achieves the best mean ranking and improvement score on NYU-v2 while remaining competitive on other benchmarks.
dataset_testbed: Two-task synthetic 2D optimisation problem with one global optimum, Novel two-task synthetic 2D optimisation problem with two global optima, CelebA (40 binary facial attribute classification tasks with a CNN), NYU-v2 (depth estimation, semantic segmentation, and surface normal prediction with MTAN), CityScapes (depth estimation and semantic segmentation with MTAN), MetaWorld MT10 multi-task reinforcement learning benchmark (10 robot manipulation tasks with Soft Actor-Critic)
abstract: The multi-task learning (MTL) paradigm aims to simultaneously learn multiple tasks within a single model capturing higher-level, more general hidden patterns that are shared by the tasks. In deep learning, a significant challenge in the backpropagation training process is the design of advanced optimisers to improve the convergence speed and stability of the gradient descent learning rule. In particular, in multi-task deep learning (MTDL) the multitude of tasks may generate potentially conflicting gradients that would hinder the concurrent convergence of the diverse loss functions. This challenge arises when the gradients of the task objectives have either different magnitudes or opposite directions, causing one or a few to dominate or to interfere with each other, thus degrading the training process. Gradient surgery methods address the problem explicitly dealing with conflicting gradients by adjusting the overall gradient trajectory. This work introduces a novel gradient surgery method, the Similarity-Aware Momentum Gradient Surgery (SAM-GS), which provides an effective and scalable approach based on a gradient magnitude similarity measure to guide the optimisation process. The SAM-GS surgery adopts gradient equalisation and modulation of the first-order momentum. A series of experimental tests have shown the effectiveness of SAM-GS on synthetic problems and MTL benchmarks. Gradient magnitude similarity plays a crucial role in regularising gradient aggregation in MTDL for the optimisation of the learning process. Code is available at https://unibzmlgroup.github.io/SAMGS/

title: Uniform Loss vs. Specialized Optimization: A Comparative Analysis in Multi-Task Learning
venue: arXiv
algorithm_or_model: Evaluation of 16 SMTOs, including Nash-MTL, CAGrad, IMTL, and FAMO, against uniform loss (Unitary Scalarization)
role_in_thesis: Provides a systematic evaluation showing that specialized optimizers surpass uniform weighting primarily on complex task configurations where severe gradient magnitude disparities occur.
problem: Recent critiques question whether specialized multi-task optimizers outperform uniform loss because previous comparisons lacked standardized evaluation and sufficient hyperparameter tuning.
proposed_solution: The authors evaluate sixteen specialized multi-task optimizers against tuned uniform loss baselines across multiple datasets with increasing multi-task balancing complexity.
claim: SMTOs clearly outperform uniform loss once multi-task problems become complex enough, although well-chosen fixed weights can still match them.
dataset_testbed: Multi-MNIST, Cityscapes, QM9, AMD Ryzen 9 5950X CPU with two NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPUs
abstract: Specialized Multi-Task Optimizers (SMTOs) balance task learning in Multi-Task Learning by addressing issues like conflicting gradients and differing gradient norms, which hinder equal-weighted task training. However, recent critiques suggest that equally weighted tasks can achieve competitive results compared to SMTOs, arguing that previous SMTO results were influenced by poor hyperparameter optimization and lack of regularization. In this work, we evaluate these claims through an extensive empirical evaluation of SMTOs, including some of the latest methods, on more complex multi-task problems to clarify this behavior. More specifically, we start our analysis by evaluating all SMTOs on a simple MNIST problem to identify the promising optimizers and assess them further on progressively more complex multi-task problems. Our findings indicate that SMTOs perform well compared to uniform loss and that fixed weights can achieve competitive performance compared to SMTOs. Furthermore, we demonstrate why uniform loss performs similarly to SMTOs in some instances. The source code is available at [https://github.com/Gabriel-SGama/UnitScal\_vs\_SMTOs](https://github.com/Gabriel-SGama/UnitScal_vs_SMTOs "").

title: Examining Common Paradigms in Multi-Task Learning
venue: 46th German Conference for Pattern Recognition (GCPR 2024)
role_in_thesis: Reveals that optimizer selection often dominates weighting methods and demonstrates that within-task sample gradient conflicts occur as frequently as cross-task conflicts.
problem: Multi-task learning methods often fail to beat single-task baselines because researchers neglect optimizer choice and assume gradient conflicts are unique to multi-task learning.
proposed_solution: The authors evaluate optimizers across multi-task benchmarks, derive loss-scale invariance for Adam and uncertainty weighting, and compare inter-task gradient conflicts with inter-sample conflicts.
claim: The optimizer choice often matters more than the multi-task method, and differences in gradient magnitude rather than gradient alignment distinguish multi-task learning from single-task learning.
dataset_testbed: Cityscapes, NYUv2, CelebA, SegNet, DeepLabV3+, ResNet-18, synthetic two-task toy regression problem, corrupted Cityscapes, corrupted NYUv2, Bosch GPU clusters
abstract: While multi-task learning (MTL) has gained significant attention in recent years, its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Recent methods did not yield consistent performance improvements over single task learning (STL) baselines, underscoring the importance of gaining more profound insights about challenges specific to MTL. In our study, we investigate paradigms in MTL in the context of STL: First, the impact of the choice of optimizer has only been mildly investigated in MTL. We show the pivotal role of common STL tools such as the Adam optimizer in MTL empirically in various experiments. To further investigate Adam’s effectiveness, we theoretical derive a partial loss-scale invariance under mild assumptions. Second, the notion of gradient conflicts has often been phrased as a specific problem in MTL. We explore the role of gradient conflicts in MTL and compare it to STL. For angular gradient alignment we find no evidence that this is a unique problem in MTL. We emphasize differences in gradient magnitude as the main distinguishing factor. Overall, we find surprising similarities between STL and MTL suggesting to consider methods from both fields in a broader context.

title: LibMTL: A Python Library for Deep Multi-Task Learning
venue: Journal of Machine Learning Research
role_in_thesis: Delivers the unified open-source PyTorch benchmarking library that implements multi-task architectures and optimization strategies to ensure standardized experimental comparison.
problem: State-of-the-art multi-task learning models are implemented in incompatible frameworks with inconsistent experimental details or lack public implementations, which makes it hard to extend them to real applications or to compare new MTL models against them fairly.
proposed_solution: The authors develop LibMTL, an open-source Python library built on PyTorch that unifies different MTL settings and provides a modular, reproducible, and extensible framework supporting 13 optimization strategies and 8 MTL architectures.
claim: LibMTL offers a more comprehensive and up-to-date unified framework than existing MTL libraries, covering more MTL settings and more state-of-the-art deep MTL methods, and enabling fair comparisons and rapid development of new MTL models.
dataset_testbed: NYUv2
abstract: This paper presents `LibMTL` , an open-source `Python` library built on `PyTorch` , which provides a unified, comprehensive, reproducible, and extensible implementation framework for Multi-Task Learning (MTL). `LibMTL` considers different settings and approaches in MTL, and it supports a large number of state-of-the-art MTL methods, including 13 optimization strategies and 8 architectures. Moreover, the modular design in `LibMTL` makes it easy to use and well extensible, thus users can easily and fast develop new MTL methods, compare with existing MTL methods fairly, or apply MTL algorithms to real-world applications with the support of `LibMTL` . The source code and detailed documentations of `LibMTL` are available at `https://github.com/median-research-group/LibMTL` and `https://libmtl.readthedocs.io` , respectively.

title: FAMO: Fast Adaptive Multitask Optimization
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36 (NeurIPS 2023)
role_in_thesis: Contributes the benchmarked FAMO algorithm that equalizes task loss decrease rates with constant memory overhead and a single backward pass.
problem: Average loss optimization in multitask learning under-optimizes some tasks, and existing gradient manipulation methods require storing all task gradients with high computation cost.
proposed_solution: The authors propose FAMO, an adaptive task weighting optimizer that balances loss decrease rates across tasks using loss history with constant time and memory overhead.
claim: FAMO matches or outperforms existing gradient manipulation methods across supervised and reinforcement learning benchmarks while drastically reducing training time and memory requirements.
dataset_testbed: NYU-v2, CityScapes, QM-9, CelebA, MetaWorld MT10, toy 2-task optimization problem
abstract: One of the grand enduring goals of AI is to create generalist agents that can learn multiple different tasks from diverse data via multitask learning (MTL). However, in practice, applying gradient descent (GD) on the average loss across all tasks may yield poor multitask performance due to severe under-optimization of certain tasks. Previous approaches that manipulate task gradients for a more balanced loss decrease require storing and computing all task gradients (𝒪⁡(k)\mathcal{O}(k) space and time where kk is the number of tasks), limiting their use in large-scale scenarios. In this work, we introduce Fast Adaptive Multitask Optimization (FAMO), a dynamic weighting method that decreases task losses in a balanced way using 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) space and time. We conduct an extensive set of experiments covering multi-task supervised and reinforcement learning problems. Our results indicate that FAMO achieves comparable or superior performance to state-of-the-art gradient manipulation techniques while offering significant improvements in space and computational efficiency. Code is available at [https://github.com/Cranial-XIX/FAMO](https://github.com/Cranial-XIX/FAMO "").

title: Independent Component Alignment for Multi-Task Learning
venue: Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR 2023)
role_in_thesis: Develops Aligned-MTL to resolve gradient conflicts by aligning orthogonal singular value components while guaranteeing convergence to user-specified task trade-off weights.
problem: Training a single model on multiple tasks is destabilized by conflicting and dominating task gradients when optimizing the averaged objective, and existing multi-task gradient methods converge to arbitrary Pareto-stationary points so that task trade-offs cannot be specified in advance.
proposed_solution: The authors use the condition number of the gradient matrix as a stability criterion for multi-task optimization and propose Aligned-MTL, which aligns the principal components of the linear system of gradients via singular value decomposition so the condition number is minimized and the resulting cumulative gradient respects pre-defined task weights.
claim: Aligned-MTL consistently outperforms prior multi-task optimization methods on scene understanding and multi-task reinforcement learning benchmarks while provably converging to an optimum with pre-defined task weights, giving more control over the optimization result.
dataset_testbed: synthetic two-task MTL benchmark, Cityscapes, NYUv2, MetaWorld MT10
abstract: In a multi-task learning (MTL) setting, a single model is trained to tackle a diverse set of tasks jointly. Despite rapid progress in the field, MTL remains challenging due to optimization issues such as conflicting and dominating gradients. In this work, we propose using a condition number of a linear system of gradients as a stability criterion of an MTL optimization. We theoretically demonstrate that a condition number reflects the aforementioned optimization issues. Accordingly, we present Aligned-MTL, a novel MTL optimization approach based on the proposed criterion, that eliminates instability in the training process by aligning the orthogonal components of the linear system of gradients. While many recent MTL approaches guarantee convergence to a minimum, task trade-offs cannot be specified in advance. In contrast, Aligned-MTL provably converges to an optimal point with pre-defined task-specific weights, which provides more control over the optimization result. Through experiments, we show that the proposed approach consistently improves performance on a diverse set of MTL benchmarks, including semantic and instance segmentation, depth estimation, surface normal estimation, and reinforcement learning. The source code is publicly available at [https://github.com/SamsungLabs/MTL](https://github.com/SamsungLabs/MTL "").

title: In Defense of the Unitary Scalarization for Deep Multi-Task Learning
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 35 (NeurIPS 2022)
algorithm_or_model: unitary scalarization coupled with standard regularization and stabilization techniques
role_in_thesis: Challenges specialized multi-task optimizers by demonstrating that unitary scalarization combined with standard single-task regularizers matches complex dynamic weighting schemes across standard benchmarks.
problem: Deep multi-task learning research increasingly argues that unitary scalarization, simply minimizing the sum of per-task losses, underperforms specialized multi-task optimizers, and the authors attribute this reported weakness to experimental variability and insufficient regularization rather than to inherent optimization difficulty.
proposed_solution: The authors benchmark popular specialized multi-task optimizers against unitary scalarization in a unified experimental pipeline across supervised and reinforcement learning settings, coupling the simple baseline with standard single-task regularization and stabilization techniques, and provide an empirical and technical analysis suggesting that many specialized optimizers act as regularizers.
claim: No specialized multi-task optimizer consistently outperforms unitary scalarization across popular supervised and reinforcement learning benchmarks once the simple baseline is combined with standard regularization and stabilization, and many specialized optimizers can be partly interpreted as forms of regularization.
dataset_testbed: Multi-MNIST, CelebA, Cityscapes, Meta-World (MT10 and MT50)
abstract: Recent multi-task learning research argues against *unitary scalarization*, where training simply minimizes the sum of the task losses. Several ad-hoc multi-task optimization algorithms have instead been proposed, inspired by various hypotheses about what makes multi-task settings difficult. The majority of these optimizers require per-task gradients, and introduce significant memory, runtime, and implementation overhead. We show that unitary scalarization, coupled with standard regularization and stabilization techniques from single-task learning, matches or improves upon the performance of complex multi-task optimizers in popular supervised and reinforcement learning settings. We then present an analysis suggesting that many specialized multi-task optimizers can be partly interpreted as forms of regularization, potentially explaining our surprising results. We believe our results call for a critical reevaluation of recent research in the area.

title: Multi-Task Learning as a Bargaining Game
venue: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML)
role_in_thesis: Introduces the benchmarked Nash-MTL algorithm that frames multi-task gradient aggregation as a cooperative bargaining game to determine a Pareto optimal update direction.
problem: In multi-task learning, per-task gradients can conflict in direction or differ in magnitude, causing a jointly trained model to perform worse than dedicated single-task models.
proposed_solution: The authors model gradient aggregation as a cooperative bargaining game and use the proportionally fair Nash bargaining solution as the parameter update direction.
claim: Nash-MTL achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple multi-task benchmarks while providing theoretical convergence guarantees to Pareto stationary or Pareto optimal points.
dataset_testbed: QM9, NYUv2, CityScapes, MT10 (Meta-World)
abstract: In Multi-task learning (MTL), a joint model is trained to simultaneously make predictions for several tasks. Joint training reduces computation costs and improves data efficiency; however, since the gradients of these different tasks may conflict, training a joint model for MTL often yields lower performance than its corresponding single-task counterparts. A common method for alleviating this issue is to combine per-task gradients into a joint update direction using a particular heuristic. In this paper, we propose viewing the gradients combination step as a bargaining game, where tasks negotiate to reach an agreement on a joint direction of parameter update. Under certain assumptions, the bargaining problem has a unique solution, known as the *Nash Bargaining Solution*, which we propose to use as a principled approach to multi-task learning. We describe a new MTL optimization procedure, Nash-MTL, and derive theoretical guarantees for its convergence. Empirically, we show that Nash-MTL achieves state-of-the-art results on multiple MTL benchmarks in various domains.

title: Do Current Multi-Task Optimization Methods in Deep Learning Even Help?
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 35 (NeurIPS 2022)
algorithm_or_model: scalarization with static task weights (implemented as proportional sampling)
role_in_thesis: Conducts an empirical audit demonstrating that well-tuned static scalarization matches specialized multi-task optimizers on translation and vision tasks while avoiding severe gradient computation overheads.
problem: Specialized multi-task optimization (MTO) algorithms are widely claimed to beat simply optimizing a weighted average of task losses, but their reported gains may be artifacts of under-tuned baselines and unreliable evaluation practices rather than genuinely better optimization.
proposed_solution: The authors run a large-scale empirical study comparing popular MTO algorithms against the Pareto frontier traced by sweeping static task-weight scalarization on multilingual machine translation and vision benchmarks, and they analyze how hyperparameter sensitivity and evaluation choices distort reported comparisons.
claim: Across language and vision tasks, no tested MTO algorithm improves on a well-tuned scalarization sweep, whose solutions form a superset of MTO solutions, and apparent MTO gains largely stem from under-tuned baselines and evaluation pitfalls.
dataset_testbed: Multilingual machine translation data for English→French, English→Chinese, English→German, and English→Romanian translation, CityScapes, CelebA, Multi-MNIST, Google Cloud Platform v3 TPUs, Nvidia A100 GPUs
abstract: Recent research has proposed a series of specialized optimization algorithms for deep multi-task models. It is often claimed that these multi-task optimization (MTO) methods yield solutions that are superior to the ones found by simply optimizing a weighted average of the task losses. In this paper, we perform large-scale experiments on a variety of language and vision tasks to examine the empirical validity of these claims. We show that, despite the added design and computational complexity of these algorithms, MTO methods do not yield any performance improvements beyond what is achievable via traditional optimization approaches. We highlight alternative strategies that consistently yield improvements to the performance profile and point out common training pitfalls that might cause suboptimal results. Finally, we outline challenges in reliably evaluating the performance of MTO algorithms and discuss potential solutions.

title: Conflict-Averse Gradient Descent for Multi-task Learning
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 34 (NeurIPS 2021)
role_in_thesis: Establishes the benchmarked CAGrad algorithm that optimizes the worst-case local task improvement within a constrained trust region around the average gradient vector.
problem: Directly minimizing the average loss in multi-task learning is undermined by conflicting task gradients, and prior gradient-manipulation heuristics lack convergence guarantees to a minimum of the average loss.
proposed_solution: The authors propose CAGrad, which at each step searches within a neighborhood of the averaged gradient for an update vector that maximizes the worst-case local improvement across task losses, provably converging to a stationary point of the average loss.
claim: CAGrad improves over prior state-of-the-art gradient manipulation methods on multi-task supervised, semi-supervised, and reinforcement learning benchmarks while provably converging to an optimum of the average loss.
dataset_testbed: Toy two-task optimization example, Multi-Fashion+MNIST with a shrinked LeNet, NYU-v2 with MTAN (SegNet backbone), CityScapes with MTAN (SegNet backbone), Meta-World MT10 with Soft Actor-Critic, Meta-World MT50 with Soft Actor-Critic, CIFAR10 semi-supervised learning with ARML (WRN-28-2 backbone)
abstract: The goal of multi-task learning is to enable more efficient learning than single task learning by sharing model structures for a diverse set of tasks. A standard multi-task learning objective is to minimize the average loss across all tasks. While straightforward, using this objective often results in much worse final performance for each task than learning them independently. A major challenge in optimizing a multi-task model is the *conflicting gradients*, where gradients of different task objectives are not well aligned so that following the average gradient direction can be detrimental to specific tasks’ performance. Previous work has proposed several heuristics to manipulate the task gradients for mitigating this problem. But most of them lack convergence guarantee and/or could converge to any Pareto-stationary point. In this paper, we introduce Conflict-Averse Gradient descent (CAGrad) which minimizes the average loss function, while leveraging the worst local improvement of individual tasks to regularize the algorithm trajectory. CAGrad balances the objectives automatically and still provably converges to a minimum over the average loss. It includes the regular gradient descent (GD) and the multiple gradient descent algorithm (MGDA) in the multi-objective optimization (MOO) literature as special cases. On a series of challenging multi-task supervised learning and reinforcement learning tasks, CAGrad achieves improved performance over prior state-of-the-art multi-objective gradient manipulation methods. Code is available at [https://github.com/Cranial-XIX/CAGrad](https://github.com/Cranial-XIX/CAGrad "").

title: TOWARDS IMPARTIAL MULTI-TASK LEARNING
venue: International Conference on Learning Representations
role_in_thesis: Provides the benchmarked IMTL algorithm that ensures scale-invariant learning by enforcing equal gradient projections for shared parameters and dynamically balancing task loss magnitudes.
problem: Training multiple tasks simultaneously in multi-task learning causes some tasks to be learned well while others are overlooked, because tasks have different loss scales and gradient magnitudes and compete with each other.
proposed_solution: The authors propose impartial multi-task learning (IMTL), which combines a closed-form gradient balance method (IMTL-G) that gives the aggregated gradient equal projections onto each task for shared parameters with a learnable loss balance method (IMTL-L) that keeps task-specific losses at a comparable scale.
claim: Combining gradient balance for task-shared parameters with loss balance for task-specific parameters yields impartial, scale-invariant multi-task learning that outperforms existing loss weighting methods on Cityscapes, NYUv2, and CelebA, and is the most robust to loss scale changes.
dataset_testbed: Cityscapes, NYUv2, CelebA
abstract: Multi-task learning (MTL) has been widely used in representation learning. However, na¨ıvely training all tasks simultaneously may lead to the partial training issue, where specific tasks are trained more adequately than others. In this paper, we propose to learn multiple tasks impartially. Specifically, for the _task-shared_ parameters, we optimize the scaling factors via a closed-form solution, such that the aggregated gradient (sum of raw gradients weighted by the scaling factors) has equal projections onto individual tasks. For the _task-specific_ parameters, we dynamically weigh the task losses so that all of them are kept at a comparable scale. Further, we find the above _gradient_ balance and _loss_ balance are complementary and thus propose a hybrid balance method to further improve the performance. Our impartial multi-task learning (IMTL) can be end-to-end trained without any heuristic hyper-parameter tuning, and is general to be applied on all kinds of losses without any distribution assumption. Moreover, our IMTL can converge to similar results even when the task losses are designed to have different scales, and thus it is scale-invariant. We extensively evaluate our IMTL on the standard MTL benchmarks including Cityscapes, NYUv2 and CelebA. It outperforms existing loss weighting methods under the same experimental settings.

title: Gradient Surgery for Multi-Task Learning
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33 (NeurIPS 2020)
role_in_thesis: Introduces the benchmarked PCGrad algorithm that projects conflicting task gradients onto the normal planes of one another to reduce destructive gradient interference.
problem: Jointly training multiple tasks often degrades performance and data efficiency because conflicting gradients, dominating gradient magnitudes, and high loss curvature cause destructive gradient interference.
proposed_solution: The authors propose PCGrad, which detects conflicting task gradients by negative cosine similarity and projects each conflicting gradient onto the normal plane of the other.
claim: PCGrad significantly improves optimization speed, data efficiency, and final performance across multi-task supervised and reinforcement learning benchmarks, while combining effectively with existing multi-task network architectures.
dataset_testbed: MultiMNIST, CityScapes, CelebA, CIFAR-100, NYUv2, Meta-World MT10 benchmark, Meta-World MT50 benchmark, Meta-World Sawyer robot pushing task, NVIDIA TITAN RTX GPU
abstract: While deep learning and deep reinforcement learning (RL) systems have demonstrated impressive results in domains such as image classification, game playing, and robotic control, data efficiency remains a major challenge. Multi-task learning has emerged as a promising approach for sharing structure across multiple tasks to enable more efficient learning. However, the multi-task setting presents a number of optimization challenges, making it difficult to realize large efficiency gains compared to learning tasks independently. The reasons why multi-task learning is so challenging compared to single-task learning are not fully understood. In this work, we identify a set of three conditions of the multi-task optimization landscape that cause detrimental gradient interference, and develop a simple yet general approach for avoiding such interference between task gradients. We propose a form of gradient surgery that projects a task’s gradient onto the normal plane of the gradient of any other task that has a *conflicting* gradient. On a series of challenging multi-task supervised and multi-task RL problems, this approach leads to substantial gains in efficiency and performance. Further, it is model-agnostic and can be combined with previously-proposed multi-task architectures for enhanced performance.

title: End-to-End Multi-Task Learning with Attention
venue: Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR 2019)
role_in_thesis: Introduces Dynamic Weight Average as a foundational heuristic that balances task losses using relative descending rates calculated from preceding training epochs without extra backpropagation passes.
problem: Multi-task networks must learn both task-shared and task-specific features while balancing each task's contribution to the loss, yet most existing approaches address only one of these challenges and scale poorly in parameters as tasks are added.
proposed_solution: The authors propose MTAN, a single shared network holding a global feature pool with a soft attention module per task at each layer that learns task-specific masks over the shared features end-to-end, together with a simple adaptive loss-weighting scheme called Dynamic Weight Average.
claim: MTAN matches or outperforms existing multi-task architectures on dense prediction and classification benchmarks while using far fewer parameters and remaining robust to the choice of loss-weighting scheme.
dataset_testbed: CityScapes, NYUv2, Visual Decathlon Challenge
abstract: We propose a novel multi-task learning architecture, which allows learning of task-specific feature-level attention. Our design, the Multi-Task Attention Network (MTAN), consists of a single shared network containing a global feature pool, together with a soft-attention module for each task. These modules allow for learning of task-specific features from the global features, whilst simultaneously allowing for features to be shared across different tasks. The architecture can be trained end-to-end and can be built upon any feed-forward neural network, is simple to implement, and is parameter efficient. We evaluate our approach on a variety of datasets, across both image-to-image predictions and image classification tasks. We show that our architecture is state-of-the-art in multi-task learning compared to existing methods, and is also less sensitive to various weighting schemes in the multi-task loss function. Code is available at [https://github.com/lorenmt/mtan](https://github.com/lorenmt/mtan "").

title: GradNorm: Gradient Normalization for Adaptive Loss Balancing in Deep Multitask Networks
venue: Proceedings of the 35th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2018)
role_in_thesis: Supplies the benchmarked GradNorm algorithm that balances gradient magnitudes across tasks according to relative inverse training rates at the shared layers.
problem: Training deep multitask networks is hard because task imbalances cause gradient magnitude imbalances that let dominant tasks overwhelm shared feature learning.
proposed_solution: The authors propose GradNorm to dynamically balance gradient magnitudes across tasks by adjusting multitask loss weights according to relative training rates.
claim: GradNorm improves multitask accuracy and reduces overfitting across multiple vision tasks while matching or exceeding the performance of exhaustive grid search.
dataset_testbed: synthetic toy multitask regression system (2-task and 10-task), NYUv2+seg (NYUv2 with depth, surface normals, and 13-class segmentation labels), NYUv2+kpts (augmented NYUv2 with depth, surface normals, and human-annotated room keypoints, ~90,000 images), Multitask Facial Landmark (MTFL) dataset, VGG16 SegNet (29M parameters), Thin ResNet-50 FCN (15M parameters), 4x Titan X GTX 12GB GPUs
abstract: Deep multitask networks, in which one neural network produces multiple predictive outputs, can offer better speed and performance than their single-task counterparts but are challenging to train properly. We present a gradient normalization (GradNorm) algorithm that automatically balances training in deep multitask models by dynamically tuning gradient magnitudes. We show that for various network architectures, for both regression and classification tasks, and on both synthetic and real datasets, GradNorm improves accuracy and reduces overfitting across multiple tasks when compared to single-task networks, static baselines, and other adaptive multitask loss balancing techniques. GradNorm also matches or surpasses the performance of exhaustive grid search methods, despite only involving a single asymmetry hyperparameter α\alpha. Thus, what was once a tedious search process that incurred exponentially more compute for each task added can now be accomplished within a few training runs, irrespective of the number of tasks. Ultimately, we will demonstrate that gradient manipulation affords us great control over the training dynamics of multitask networks and may be one of the keys to unlocking the potential of multitask learning.

title: Multi-Task Learning Using Uncertainty to Weigh Losses for Scene Geometry and Semantics
venue: Proceedings of the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR 2018)
algorithm_or_model: homoscedastic uncertainty-weighted multi-task loss with a DeepLabV3/ResNet101 encoder-decoder scene understanding network
role_in_thesis: Provides the benchmarked uncertainty weighting algorithm that dynamically scales task losses using learned homoscedastic task variance parameters.
problem: Multi-task deep learning performance depends strongly on the relative weighting between each task's loss, and hand-tuning these weights is expensive and difficult, which makes multi-task learning impractical.
proposed_solution: The authors derive a principled multi-task loss function that automatically learns the relative weights of multiple classification and regression losses by maximizing the likelihood of each task under its homoscedastic (task-dependent) uncertainty.
claim: Weighting task losses by learned homoscedastic uncertainty allows a single model to jointly learn semantic segmentation, instance segmentation, and per-pixel depth regression while outperforming separately trained single-task models.
dataset_testbed: CityScapes, Tiny CityScapes (downsampled to 128x256 resolution), NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1080Ti GPU
abstract: Numerous deep learning applications benefit from multi-task learning with multiple regression and classification objectives. In this paper we make the observation that the performance of such systems is strongly dependent on the relative weighting between each task’s loss. Tuning these weights by hand is a difficult and expensive process, making multi-task learning prohibitive in practice. We propose a principled approach to multi-task deep learning which weighs multiple loss functions by considering the homoscedastic uncertainty of each task. This allows us to simultaneously learn various quantities with different units or scales in both classification and regression settings. We demonstrate our model learning per-pixel depth regression, semantic and instance segmentation from a monocular input image. Perhaps surprisingly, we show our model can learn multi-task weightings and outperform separate models trained individually on each task.

title: Multi-Task Learning as Multi-Objective Optimization
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 31 (NeurIPS 2018)
algorithm_or_model: MGDA-UB (Multiple Gradient Descent Algorithm - Upper Bound)
role_in_thesis: Provides the foundational multi-objective optimization framework that adapts multiple gradient descent to locate Pareto-stationary solutions with an efficient representation-level upper bound.
problem: The common practice of minimizing a weighted linear combination of per-task losses in multi-task learning is only valid when tasks do not compete, but real tasks often conflict, so a trade-off between them must be modeled rather than approximated by a fixed weighted sum.
proposed_solution: The authors recast multi-task learning as multi-objective optimization aimed at finding a Pareto optimal solution, using a Frank-Wolfe-based solver for the multiple gradient descent algorithm together with an upper-bound objective (MGDA-UB) computed from gradients with respect to shared representations so that everything runs with a single backward pass and negligible overhead.
claim: Treating multi-task learning explicitly as multi-objective optimization yields models that outperform recent multi-task formulations, uncertainty weighting, GradNorm, and per-task training across digit classification, multi-label classification, and scene understanding, while adding negligible computational overhead.
dataset_testbed: MultiMNIST, CelebA, Cityscapes, Titan Xp GPU
abstract: In multi-task learning, multiple tasks are solved jointly, sharing inductive bias between them. Multi-task learning is inherently a multi-objective problem because different tasks may conflict, necessitating a trade-off. A common compromise is to optimize a proxy objective that minimizes a weighted linear combination of per-task losses. However, this workaround is only valid when the tasks do not compete, which is rarely the case. In this paper, we explicitly cast multi-task learning as multi-objective optimization, with the overall objective of finding a Pareto optimal solution. To this end, we use algorithms developed in the gradient-based multi-objective optimization literature. These algorithms are not directly applicable to large-scale learning problems since they scale poorly with the dimensionality of the gradients and the number of tasks. We therefore propose an upper bound for the multi-objective loss and show that it can be optimized efficiently. We further prove that optimizing this upper bound yields a Pareto optimal solution under realistic assumptions. We apply our method to a variety of multi-task deep learning problems including digit classification, scene understanding (joint semantic segmentation, instance segmentation, and depth estimation), and multi-label classification. Our method produces higher-performing models than recent multi-task learning formulations or per-task training.

title: Multitask Learning
venue: Machine Learning
algorithm_or_model: Multitask Learning (MTL) in backpropagation nets, plus MTL algorithms for k-nearest neighbor, kernel regression, and decision trees
role_in_thesis: Establishes the foundational hard parameter sharing paradigm that enables concurrent multi-task training over a single shared encoder to improve generalization through inductive transfer.
problem: Learning each task in isolation ignores the domain information available in the training signals of related tasks drawn from the same domain, causing tabula rasa learners to generalize poorly on difficult real-world problems.
proposed_solution: Train multiple related tasks in parallel on one learner that shares an internal representation (e.g., extra outputs on a backprop net with a shared hidden layer), so the extra task training signals act as an inductive bias that improves generalization on the main task.
claim: Across simulated and real domains (road following, door recognition, pneumonia risk prediction, robot sensing, and synthetic functions), training related tasks in parallel on a shared representation cut generalization error on the main task by roughly 5-40%, and shuffle tests confirmed the gains come from information in the extra training signals rather than side effects of having multiple outputs.
dataset_testbed: 1D-ALVINN synthetic road image domain, 1D-DOORS real door image domain collected with a robot-mounted camera, Medis Pneumonia Database (14,199 pneumonia cases from 78 hospitals), Peaks Functions (120 synthetic conditional functions), Xavier robot sensory prediction domain, synthetic F1/F2 sigmoid function problems
abstract: Multitask Learning is an approach to inductive transfer that improves generalization by using the domain information contained in the training signals of _related_ tasks as an inductive bias. It does this by learning tasks in parallel while using a shared representation; what is learned for each task can help other tasks be learned better. This paper reviews prior work on MTL, presents new evidence that MTL in backprop nets discovers task relatedness without the need of supervisory signals, and presents new results for MTL with k-nearest neighbor and kernel regression. In this paper we demonstrate multitask learning in three domains. We explain how multitask learning works, and show that there are many opportunities for multitask learning in real domains. We present an algorithm and results for multitask learning with case-based methods like k-nearest neighbor and kernel regression, and sketch an algorithm for multitask learning in decision trees. Because multitask learning works, can be applied to many different kinds of domains, and can be used with different learning algorithms, we conjecture there will be many opportunities for its use on real-world problems.

title: CrisisSense-LLM: Instruction Fine-Tuned Large Language Model for Multi-label Social Media Text Classification in Disaster Informatics
venue: Advanced Engineering Informatics
role_in_thesis: Proves that instruction fine-tuning enables a unified architecture to classify multiple disaster dimensions simultaneously rather than using separate models.
problem: Disaster text classification studies usually train one model per label, which creates redundancy and inefficiency, and general pre-trained LLMs lack the disaster-specific knowledge needed for reliable use on these tasks.
proposed_solution: The authors build an instruction dataset of over 60,000 labeled disaster tweets and use it to instruction fine-tune the open-source LLaMA2 model so that one model predicts event type, informativeness, and human aid type at the same time.
claim: Instruction fine-tuning a single LLM for simultaneous multi-label disaster tweet classification raises overall accuracy to 63.8 percent, nearly 15 times better than the zero-shot baseline models.
dataset_testbed: CrisisBench disaster tweet dataset, computation node with 3 A40 GPUs for LoRA fine-tuning, computation node with 16 A100 GPUs for full parameter tuning
abstract: In the field of crisis/disaster informatics, social media is increasingly being used for improving situational awareness to inform response and relief efforts. Efficient and accurate text classification tools have been a focal area of investigation in crisis informatics. This study introduces a novel approach to disaster text classification by enhancing a pre-trained Large Language Model (LLM) through instruction fine-tuning targeted for multi-label classification of disaster-related tweets. Our methodology involves creating a comprehensive instruction dataset with more than 60,000 samples from disaster-related tweets, which is then used to fine-tune an open-source LLM, thereby embedding it with disaster-specific knowledge. This fine-tuned model can classify multiple aspects of disaster-related information simultaneously, such as the type of event, informativeness, and involvement of human aid, significantly improving the utility of social media data for situational awareness in disasters. Our results show a significant improvement in categorizing critical information, with an overall accuracy of 63.8% across multiple labels. The overall accuracy of the fine-tuned model is nearly 15 times better than baseline models, whose overall accuracy is 4.27%, demonstrating its effectiveness in enhancing situational awareness. This research paves the way for more advanced, adaptable, and robust disaster management tools, leveraging the capabilities of LLMs to improve real-time situational awareness and response strategies in disaster scenarios. The source code and data relevant to this work is openly accessible in https://github.com/KaiYin97/CrsisLLM

title: Generalizing to Unseen Disaster Events: A Causal View
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: AACL-IJCNLP 2025
algorithm_or_model: Causal debiasing framework with domain-specific experts and bias model
role_in_thesis: Analyzes event-specific spurious correlations and demonstrates how debiasing strategies enhance generalization to emerging, unseen disaster events.
problem: Classifiers for disaster posts rely on spurious event-specific and domain-specific cues from past events, which hurts generalization to emerging disaster events.
proposed_solution: The authors propose a causal debiasing framework that combines an event bias model, domain-specific attention experts, and masking augmentation.
claim: The proposed causal debiasing framework outperforms all baselines across three disaster classification tasks under temporal splits to unseen events.
dataset_testbed: HumAID, CrisisLex T26, Trecis (TREC Incident Streams), NVIDIA A100 GPU (40GB)
abstract: Due to the rapid growth of social media platforms, these tools have become essential for monitoring information during ongoing disaster events. However, extracting valuable insights requires real-time processing of vast amounts of data. A major challenge in existing systems is their exposure to event-related biases, which negatively affects their ability to generalize to emerging events. While recent advancements in debiasing and causal learning offer promising solutions, they remain underexplored in the disaster event domain. In this work, we approach bias mitigation through a causal lens and propose a method to reduce event- and domain-related biases, enhancing generalization to future events. Our approach outperforms multiple baselines by up to +1.9% F1 and significantly improves a PLM-based classifier across three disaster classification tasks.

title: Detecting Actionable Requests and Offers on Social Media During Crises Using LLMs
venue: Proceedings of the 22nd International Conference on Information Systems for Crisis Response and Management (ISCRAM 2025)
role_in_thesis: Develops a fine-grained hierarchical taxonomy and retrieval-augmented prompting for actionability and resource triage during disasters.
problem: Existing crisis social media systems classify posts only at a coarse request versus offer level with single labels, and supervised models need costly human annotation that is hard to obtain during disasters.
proposed_solution: The authors build a fine-grained hierarchical taxonomy of supplies, actions, and emergency personnel and classify posts with instruction-tuned LLMs using QSF Learning, a RAG-based prompting method that retrieves query-specific labeled examples for each input message.
claim: QSF Learning consistently beats static baseline prompting strategies across models and datasets, with the largest gains on the complex actions and personnel tasks.
dataset_testbed: Synthetic dataset of 1,346 disaster tweets generated with GPT-4o, 300 manually annotated Hurricane Sandy tweets from Purohit et al. 2014, later improved by Lamsal et al. 2024
abstract: Natural disasters often result in a surge of social media activity, including requests for assistance, offers of help, sentiments, and general updates. To enable humanitarian organizations to respond more efficiently, we propose a fine-grained hierarchical taxonomy to systematically organize crisis-related information about requests and offers into three critical dimensions: supplies, emergency personnel, and actions. Leveraging the capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs), we introduce Query-Specific Few-shot Learning (QSF Learning) that retrieves class-specific labeled examples from an embedding database to enhance the model's performance in detecting and classifying posts. Beyond classification, we assess the actionability of messages to prioritize posts requiring immediate attention. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms baseline prompting strategies, effectively identifying and prioritizing actionable requests and offers.

title: CrisisTransformers: Pre-trained language models and sentence encoders for crisis-related social media texts
venue: Knowledge-Based Systems
algorithm_or_model: CrisisTransformers (CT-M1, CT-M2, CT-M3 pre-trained models and their sentence encoder variants)
role_in_thesis: Introduces domain-specific pretrained transformer encoders that outperform generic language models across eighteen crisis informatics benchmarks.
problem: Existing pre-trained language models and general-purpose sentence encoders are not tailored to the informal language of crisis-related social media texts, which limits the automated analysis that emergency responders need.
proposed_solution: The authors pre-train BERT-base sized models called CrisisTransformers on a 15 billion token corpus of crisis tweets and adapt them into sentence encoders with contrastive learning.
claim: Domain-specific pre-training on crisis tweets produces models that beat strong general-purpose baselines on all 18 crisis classification datasets and lifts the sentence encoding state of the art by 17.43 percent.
dataset_testbed: Crisis corpus of over 15 billion word tokens from tweets on more than 30 crisis events (pre-training), CrisisMMD (D-01), CrisisLex (D-02), AIDR (D-03), ISCRAM2013 (D-04), SWDM2013 (D-05), CrisisNLP (D-06), Poddar et al. (2022) COVID-19 vaccine stance dataset (D-07), SAD Stressor (D-08), SAD Stress (D-09), SAD COVID (D-10), LocBERT (D-11), HMC (a) (D-12), Cotfas et al. (2021) COVID-19 vaccination opinions dataset (D-13), HMC (b) (D-14), PHM (D-15), Klein et al. (2021) (a) (D-16), Klein et al. (2021) (b) (D-17), ANTiVax (D-18), GooAQ (question, answer pairs for MNR training), QQP (triplets with hard negatives), AllNLI, General-domain SemEval tweet datasets (Appendix A), 6 NVIDIA A100 GPUs with 80GB memory for pre-training, Intel Xeon Gold 6326 CPU with an 80GB A100 GPU for inference time analysis
abstract: Social media platforms play an essential role in crisis communication, but analyzing crisis-related social media texts is challenging due to their informal nature. Transformer-based pre-trained models like BERT and RoBERTa have shown success in various NLP tasks, but they are not tailored for crisis-related texts. Furthermore, general-purpose sentence encoders are used to generate sentence embeddings, regardless of the textual complexities in crisis-related texts. Advances in applications like text classification, semantic search, and clustering contribute to the effective processing of crisis-related texts, which is essential for emergency responders to gain a comprehensive view of a crisis event, whether historical or real-time. To address these gaps in crisis informatics literature, this study introduces CrisisTransformers, an ensemble of pre-trained language models and sentence encoders trained on an extensive corpus of over 15 billion word tokens from tweets associated with more than 30 crisis events, including disease outbreaks, natural disasters, conflicts, and other critical incidents. We evaluate existing models and CrisisTransformers on 18 crisis-specific public datasets. Our pre-trained models outperform strong baselines across all datasets in classification tasks, and our best-performing sentence encoder improves the state-of-the-art by 17.43% in sentence encoding tasks. Additionally, we investigate the impact of model initialization on convergence and evaluate the significance of domain-specific models in generating semantically meaningful sentence embeddings. The models are publicly available at: https://huggingface.co/crisistransformers

title: Evaluating Urgency of Typhoon-Related Tweets Through Sentiment Analysis Using Artificial Neural Networks
venue: International Journal of Computing Sciences Research
role_in_thesis: Grounds the disaster triage problem in Philippine typhoon response by evaluating neural models for social media urgency scoring.
problem: Responders in the Philippines cannot efficiently find urgent disaster calls on social media because government communication protocols do not standardize social media platforms.
proposed_solution: The authors train a feed-forward neural network using supervised sentiment analysis to assign urgency scores between 0 and 1 to typhoon-related tweets.
claim: The artificial neural network accurately predicts the urgency of typhoon tweets, achieving 99.17 percent validation accuracy and 99 percent accuracy on separate confusion matrix testing.
dataset_testbed: Dataset of 4,020 English and Tagalog tweets from Typhoon Ulysses collected using Tweepy and the Twitter API, split into 3,900 training and 120 validation tweets, Validation dataset of 100 tweets with 43 urgent and 57 non-urgent tweets for confusion matrix analysis
abstract:
_Purpose_ – The main objective of this project was to evaluate typhoon-related Tweets’ urgency using sentiment analysis with supervised learning over an artificial neural network.

_Method_ – The researchers implemented artificial neural network and natural language processing techniques for sentiment analysis and evaluation of the urgency score of typhoon-related Tweets. The model’s accuracy on training and validation was evaluated simultaneously. A separate validation using 100 data was done using confusion matrix analysis.

_Results_ – The accuracy of the model in training was at 99.87% and the loss was 0.0074. Validation was conducted simultaneously with the training. It was found that the accuracy of the model was at 99.17% and the loss was 0.0680. The confusion matrix analysis showed that the sensitivity was 97.67% and the specificity was 100%. The positive predictive value was 100% and the negative predicted value was 98.28%. Both false positive and false discovery rates are at 0% while the false-negative rate was at 2.33%. Finally, the F1 score was 98.82% and accuracy was 99%.

_Conclusion_ – The implementation of the architecture of the model was successful; the researchers concluded that the training produced successful results by looking at the high accuracy prediction of the model and the low loss during the simultaneous training and validation, and confusion matrix analysis for the separate validation.

_Recommendations_ – The researchers recommend expanding the vocabulary of the model by adding more diverse data to the dataset when training. The model produced by this study can be used in incident reporting systems that will be helpful during times of typhoon-related disasters.

_Research Implications_ – Using the model produced by the study in incident reporting applications of the government and NGOs will be more efficient than manually looking at typhoon-related posts on Twitter.

title: Enhancing Crisis-Related Tweet Classification with Entity-Masked Language Modeling and Multi-Task Learning
venue: NLP4PI Workshop @ EMNLP 2022
algorithm_or_model: Entity-masked language modeling (E-MLM) with hierarchical multi-task classification heads (HMCN) on BERT
role_in_thesis: Couples entity masking with multi-task learning to prevent overfitting to disaster-specific named entities and improve cross-event generalization.
problem: Crisis tweet classifiers overfit to event-specific entities and biases and face highly imbalanced labels, so they perform poorly on rare actionable information types for unseen disaster events.
proposed_solution: The authors combine adaptive pre-training with entity-masked language modeling and hierarchical multi-label classification heads trained as a multi-task problem on top of BERT.
claim: The combination of entity-masked pre-training and hierarchical multi-task learning raises actionable information type F1 by up to 10 percent and improves generalization to unseen crisis events.
dataset_testbed: TREC-IS (2020B split of crisis-related tweets)
abstract: Social media has become an important information source for crisis management and provides quick access to ongoing developments and critical information. However, classification models suffer from event-related biases and highly imbalanced label distributions which still poses a challenging task. To address these challenges, we propose a combination of entity-masked language modeling and hierarchical multi-label classification as a multi-task learning problem. We evaluate our method on tweets from the TREC-IS dataset and show an absolute performance gain w.r.t. F1-score of up to 10% for actionable information types. Moreover, we found that entity-masking reduces the effect of overfitting to in-domain events and enables improvements in cross-event generalization. Our source code is publicly available on GitHub.

title: CrisisBench: Benchmarking Crisis-related Social Media Datasets for Humanitarian Information Processing
venue: Proceedings of the International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media (ICWSM 2021)
algorithm_or_model: event-aware training with CNN, fastText, and transformer models (BERT, DistilBERT, RoBERTa)
role_in_thesis: Provides the consolidated benchmark dataset and standardized evaluation protocol for informativeness and humanitarian intent classification across multiple crisis types.
problem: Crisis informatics research lacks standard benchmark datasets because the datasets used across studies are dispersed, use inconsistent class labels, contain exact and near-duplicate content, and often lack language tags, making published results impossible to compare.
proposed_solution: The authors consolidate eight publicly available crisis tweet datasets into one standardized resource with manually mapped class labels, filtered exact and near duplicates, and per-tweet language tags, and provide benchmark results using CNN, fastText, and transformer models for informativeness and humanitarian classification.
claim: Training on the consolidated, duplicate-free dataset generalizes better than training on individual datasets, and transformer models (best: RoBERTa) set benchmarks of 0.883 weighted F1 for informativeness and 0.872 for humanitarian classification on the cleaned English tweets.
dataset_testbed: CrisisBench consolidated dataset (English tweets, new dataset built by the paper), CrisisBench consolidated multilingual dataset (preliminary experiments), CrisisLex (CrisisLexT26 and CrisisLexT6), CrisisNLP, SWDM2013, ISCRAM2013, Disaster Response Data (DRD), Disasters on Social Media (DSM), CrisisMMD, AIDR
abstract: Time-critical analysis of social media streams is important for humanitarian organizations for planing rapid response during disasters. The crisis informatics research community has developed several techniques and systems for processing and classifying big crisis-related data posted on social media. However, due to the dispersed nature of the datasets used in the literature (e.g., for training models), it is not possible to compare the results and measure the progress made towards building better models for crisis informatics tasks. In this work, we attempt to bridge this gap by combining various existing crisis-related datasets. We consolidate eight human-annotated datasets and provide 166.1k and 141.5k tweets for informativeness and humanitarian classification tasks, respectively. We believe that the consolidated dataset will help train more sophisticated models. Moreover, we provide benchmarks for both binary and multiclass classification tasks using several deep learning architecrures including, CNN, fastText, and transformers. We make the dataset and scripts available at: https://crisisnlp.qcri.org/crisis\_datasets\_benchmarks.html

title: HumAID: Human-Annotated Disaster Incidents Data from Twitter with Deep Learning Benchmarks
venue: Proceedings of the International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media (ICWSM 2021)
algorithm_or_model: SVM, Random Forest, fastText, and transformer models (BERT, RoBERTa, XLM-RoBERTa, DistilBERT)
role_in_thesis: Supplies the largest human-annotated disaster tweet corpus and establishes transformer baselines across nineteen separate disaster events.
problem: Existing labeled Twitter datasets for disaster response are small, contain exact or near duplicates, and are otherwise too limited to support data-hungry deep learning models for humanitarian information classification.
proposed_solution: The authors built HumAID, the largest human-annotated disaster tweet dataset (about 77K tweets sampled from roughly 24 million tweets covering 19 disasters) through a multi-step filtering and crowdsourced annotation pipeline, and released fixed data splits with classification baselines.
claim: HumAID is the largest publicly available human-annotated disaster tweet dataset, and the authors' experiments show transformer-based models, especially RoBERTa, outperform classical supervised algorithms, providing strong baselines for future crisis informatics research.
dataset_testbed: HumAID: newly created dataset of 77,196 human-labeled tweets across 19 disaster events (2016-2019), Pool of 24,859,155 tweets collected via the AIDR system using the Twitter streaming API, Humanitarian categories labeled data from Alam, Imran, and Ofli (2019) used to train the Random Forest filtering classifier
abstract: Social networks are widely used for information consumption and dissemination, especially during time-critical events such as natural disasters. Despite its significantly large volume, social media content is often too noisy for direct use in any application. Therefore, it is important to filter, categorize, and concisely summarize the available content to facilitate effective consumption and decision-making. To address such issues automatic classification systems have been developed using supervised modeling approaches, thanks to the earlier efforts on creating labeled datasets. However, existing datasets are limited in different aspects (e.g., size, contains duplicates) and less suitable to support more advanced and data-hungry deep learning models. In this paper, we present a new large-scale dataset with ∼{\sim}77K human-labeled tweets, sampled from a pool of ∼{\sim}24 million tweets across 19 disaster events that happened between 2016 and 2019. Moreover, we propose a data collection and sampling pipeline, which is important for social media data sampling for human annotation. We report multiclass classification results using classic and deep learning (fastText and transformer) based models to set the ground for future studies. The dataset and associated resources are publicly available.11 1 https://crisisnlp.qcri.org/humaid\_dataset.html

title: Transformer-based Multi-task Learning for Disaster Tweet Categorisation
venue: Proceedings of the 18th ISCRAM Conference – Social Media for Disaster Response and Resilience
algorithm_or_model: Transformer-based multi-task learning (MTL) with ensemble of transformer encoders
role_in_thesis: Demonstrates that multi-task transformer architectures improve joint prediction of humanitarian information types and priority levels over single-task baselines.
problem: Emergency responders need crisis-related social media messages to be automatically categorised by information type and priority, because the volume of tweets grows explosively during a disaster and manual identification of useful messages is not feasible.
proposed_solution: The authors fine-tune transformer encoders in a multi-task learning framework that jointly performs multi-label information type classification and priority estimation on disaster tweets, and further combine multiple such models through a simple ensemble of their predictions.
claim: The transformer-based multi-task approach outperforms single-task and traditional machine learning baselines, and an ensemble of four multi-task transformer models achieves state-of-the-art performance in almost every TREC-IS evaluation metric, reaching an overall harmonic mean score of 0.3141.
dataset_testbed: TREC-IS 2018, TREC-IS 2019A, TREC-IS 2019B, TREC-IS 2020A, RTX-2080Ti GPU, RTX-2070 Super GPU
abstract: Social media has enabled people to circulate information in a timely fashion, thus motivating people to post messages seeking help during crisis situations. These messages can contribute to the situational awareness of emergency responders, who have a need for them to be categorised according to information types (i.e. the type of aid services the messages are requesting). We introduce a transformer-based multi-task learning (MTL) technique for classifying information types and estimating the priority of these messages. We evaluate the effectiveness of our approach with a variety of metrics by submitting runs to the TREC Incident Streams (IS) track: a research initiative specifically designed for disaster tweet classification and prioritisation. The results demonstrate that our approach achieves competitive performance in most metrics as compared to other participating runs. Subsequently, we find that an ensemble approach combining disparate transformer encoders within our approach helps to improve the overall effectiveness to a significant extent, achieving state-of-the-art performance in almost every metric. We make the code publicly available so that our work can be reproduced and used as a baseline for the community for future work in this domain1.

title: Cross-Lingual Disaster-related Multi-label Tweet Classification with Manifold Mixup
venue: Proceedings of the 58th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Student Research Workshop
role_in_thesis: Benchmarks multilingual multi-label disaster tweet classification and verifies model generalization on unseen disasters including Philippine floods.
problem: Most prior disaster-related tweet classification work handles only English and single-label settings, and there was no large-scale standard multilingual dataset for multi-label disaster tweet classification, despite the need in disaster-prone non-English-speaking regions for real-time classifiers.
proposed_solution: The authors aggregate existing CrisisNLP and CrisisLex resources into a large multilingual multi-label dataset under a new annotation scheme, train Multilingual BERT with a class-mask-based loss that exploits partially labeled (binary-only) samples alongside multi-class samples, and further augment the model with Manifold Mixup.
claim: Multilingual BERT fine-tuned with Manifold Mixup outperforms all non-BERT baselines and consistently improves over plain M-BERT, generalizing to unseen disasters and achieving strong zero-shot transfer to unseen languages such as Spanish, French, and Italian.
dataset_testbed: Aggregated multilingual disaster tweet dataset of over 130K samples built from CrisisNLP resources #1, #4, #5, #7 and CrisisLexT6 and CrisisLexT26, Russia Meteor test set, Cyclone Pam test set, Philippines Flood test set, Mixed disasters test set
abstract: Distinguishing informative and actionable messages from a social media platform like Twitter is critical for facilitating disaster management. For this purpose, we compile a multilingual dataset of over 130K samples for multilabel classification of disaster-related tweets. We present a masking-based loss function for partially labeled samples and demonstrate the effectiveness of Manifold Mixup in the text domain. Our main model is based on Multilingual BERT, which we further improve with Manifold Mixup. We show that our model generalizes to unseen disasters in the test set. Furthermore, we analyze the capability of our model for zero-shot generalization to new languages. Our code, dataset, and other resources are available on Github.<sup>1</sup>

title: Detecting Urgency Status of Crisis Tweets: A Transfer Learning Approach for Low Resource Languages
venue: Proceedings of the 28th International Conference on Computational Linguistics
algorithm_or_model: Embedding-feature classifiers (MLP, CNN, SVM, RF) with self-training data augmentation and ensemble voting over RoBERTa, LASER, XLM-R, VecMap, and ProcB features
role_in_thesis: Validates cross-lingual transfer learning with pretrained contextual embeddings to detect urgency in low-resource disaster tweets.
problem: Crisis response needs urgent social media post detection, but automated language tools and labeled urgency data do not exist for most low-resource languages.
proposed_solution: The authors release crisis tweet urgency datasets and evaluate zero-shot cross-lingual transfer from English to Sinhala and Odia using contextual and projection embeddings.
claim: Deep contextual embeddings enable effective crisis urgency detection and zero-shot cross-lingual transfer to low-resource languages even with very small labeled datasets.
dataset_testbed: English crisis tweet urgency dataset (1,919 annotations created by the authors on Figure-Eight), Sinhala urgency evaluation dataset (LORELEI IL10, LDC2018E57, 181 natively annotated sentences), Odia urgency evaluation dataset (LORELEI IL11, LDC2019E62, 510 natively annotated sentences), Unlabeled crisis-related tweets from the Imran et al. (2016) disaster tweet collection used for self-training augmentation, English-Sinhala (415,042 sentences) and English-Odia (454,540 sentences) parallel corpora from LDC LORELEI packages used to build projection-based cross-lingual embeddings
abstract: We release an urgency dataset that consists of English tweets relating to natural crises. The set is annotated along with annotations of their corresponding urgency status. Additionally, we release evaluation datasets for two low-resource languages, i.e. Sinhala and Odia, and demonstrate an effective zero-shot transfer from English to these two languages by training cross-lingual classifiers. We adopt cross-lingual embeddings constructed using different methods to extract features of the tweets, including a few state-of-the-art contextual embeddings such as BERT, RoBERTa and XLM-R. We train a variety of classifier architectures, supervised and semi supervised, on the extracted features. We also further experiment with ensembling the various classifiers. With very limited amounts of labeled data in English and zero data in the low resource languages, we show a successful framework of training monolingual and cross-lingual classifiers using deep learning methods which are known to be data hungry. Specifically, we show that the recent deep contextual embeddings are also helpful when dealing with very small-scale datasets. Classifiers that incorporate RoBERTa yield the best performance for the English urgency detection task, with 25% F1 score absolute improvement over the baselines. For the zero-shot transfer to low resource languages, classifiers that use LASER features perform the best for Sinhala transfer while XLM-R features benefit the Odia transfer the most.

title: Twitter as a Lifeline: Human-annotated Twitter Corpora for NLP of Crisis-related Messages
venue: Proceedings of the Tenth International Conference on Language Resources and Evaluation (LREC 2016)
algorithm_or_model: Naive Bayes, Support Vector Machines, and Random Forest crisis-message classifiers
role_in_thesis: Establishes the foundational humanitarian taxonomy and crowdsourced annotation methodology for classifying crisis messages during sudden-onset disasters.
problem: Crisis-informatics researchers cannot fully exploit NLP and machine learning methods for disaster-related Twitter messages because human-annotated data for such short, noisy, informal texts is scarce.
proposed_solution: The authors collect over 52 million crisis-related tweets from 19 crises, have volunteers and paid crowdsourced workers annotate around 50,000 of them with UN OCHA-derived information categories and out-of-vocabulary normalizations, and release the corpora, trained classifiers, word2vec embeddings, and lexical resources to the research community.
claim: The released human-annotated corpora are effective for training multiclass message classifiers, with most information categories reaching acceptable AUC levels (at or above 0.80), and the resources can improve NLP for crisis messages and disaster response efforts.
dataset_testbed: Nepal Earthquake tweets, Terremoto Chile tweets, Chile Earthquake tweets, California Earthquake tweets, Pakistan Earthquake tweets, Cyclone PAM tweets, Typhoon Hagupit tweets, Hurricane Odile tweets, Iceland Volcano tweets, Landslides worldwide tweets (English), Landslides worldwide tweets (French), Landslides worldwide tweets (Spanish), Pakistan Floods tweets, India Floods tweets, Palestine Conflict tweets, Peshawar Attack Pakistan tweets, Middle East Respiratory Syndrome tweets, Ebola virus outbreak tweets, Malaysia Airlines flight MH370 tweets
abstract: Microblogging platforms such as Twitter provide active communication channels during mass convergence and emergency events such as earthquakes, typhoons. During the sudden onset of a crisis situation, affected people post useful information on Twitter that can be used for situational awareness and other humanitarian disaster response efforts, if processed timely and effectively. Processing social media information pose multiple challenges such as parsing noisy, brief and informal messages, learning information categories from the incoming stream of messages and classifying them into different classes among others. One of the basic necessities of many of these tasks is the availability of data, in particular human-annotated data. In this paper, we present human-annotated Twitter corpora collected during 19 different crises that took place between 2013 and 2015. To demonstrate the utility of the annotations, we train machine learning classifiers. Moreover, we publish first largest word2vec word embeddings trained on 52 million crisis-related tweets. To deal with tweets language issues, we present human-annotated normalized lexical resources for different lexical variations.

title: Benchmarking Open-Source Large Language Models on Code-Switched Tagalog-English Retrieval Augmented Generation
venue: Journal of Advances in Information Technology
algorithm_or_model: Five open-source LLMs (Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, SeaLLMs-v3-1.5B-Chat, Falcon-7b-instruct, Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct, Gemma-7b-it) in a LangChain and FAISS RAG pipeline
role_in_thesis: Establishes performance degradation in open-source language models when processing code-switched Taglish queries relative to standard English.
problem: It is unclear how well open-source LLMs handle Tagalog-English code-switched queries in retrieval-augmented generation, and code-switching raises the risk of hallucinated answers.
proposed_solution: The authors built a RAG question answering pipeline around five open-source LLMs and benchmarked their answers to English, Tagalog, and Taglish questions with overlap metrics and LLM-judged quality metrics.
claim: Mistral and SeaLLM clearly beat Falcon, Phi-3-mini, and Gemma at producing grounded and relevant answers for code-switched queries, while all models performed best on English, next on Taglish, and worst on Tagalog.
dataset_testbed: Curated corpus of nine .txt and .pdf documents covering news articles, short stories, and academic literature written in English, Tagalog, or Taglish, Manually built evaluation set of 15 question-answer pairs per document, grouped into five questions each in English, Tagalog, and Taglish
abstract: Code-switching, the alternation between languages within a sentence or discourse, poses significant challenges in Natural Language Processing (NLP). Effective NLP systems must employ advanced modeling techniques to accurately process and generate code-switched text, capturing the linguistic nuances and contextual dependencies. This study evaluates five open-source Large Language Models (LLMs)—Mistral, SeaLLM, Falcon, Phi-3-mini, and Gemma—on their performance with code-switched Tagalog-English (Taglish) queries in a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) task. Mistral and SeaLLM outperformed the others in generating contextually grounded and relevant answers, attributed to their advanced architectures and extensive multilingual training data. In contrast, Falcon, Phi-3-mini, and Gemma struggled with effective code-switching handling. The models performed best on English queries, followed by Taglish, with the lowest performance on Tagalog queries, highlighting the need for more balanced training data for low-resource languages. Additionally, models retrieved context better from .pdf documents compared to .txt files. Future research should focus on analyzing language composition in datasets, investigating real-world codeswitching behavior, and studying the effects of code-switching on model understanding to enhance NLP accessibility for underrepresented languages.

title: Meta-Pretraining for Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Named Entity Recognition in Low-Resource Philippine Languages
venue: Proceedings of the 5th Workshop on Multilingual Representation Learning (MRL 2025)
algorithm_or_model: First-order MAML meta-pretrained Pico decoder language models (Pico-MAML)
role_in_thesis: Demonstrates meta-pretraining techniques that enable compact decoder models to perform entity recognition on Philippine languages under strict latency constraints.
problem: Zero-shot named entity recognition in low-resource languages normally requires finetuning very large multilingual language models, which is impractical when memory or latency is constrained, and standard pretraining fails to adapt to languages with unfamiliar morphosyntactic cues.
proposed_solution: The authors propose meta-pretraining small decoder language models by replacing part of the autoregressive pretraining objective with first-order model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML) episodes, so that the initialization transfers zero-shot to unseen low-resource languages without any in-language exposure.
claim: Replacing part of autoregressive pretraining with first-order MAML lets small decoder language models improve zero-shot NER transfer to Tagalog and Cebuano by 2-6 micro-F1 percentage points under head-only tuning and 1-3 points after full tuning, with the largest gains on single-token person entities anchored by Tagalog case particles.
