dataset_testbed: Pico decoder language models (11M, 65M, 181M, 570M parameters), Pico pre-tokenized Dolma pretraining corpus, Paloma perplexity benchmark, Universal NER v1 zero-shot test sets (Tagalog tl_trg, Tagalog tl_ugnayan, Cebuano ceb_gja), Universal NER v1 high-resource finetuning sets (da_ddt, en_ewt, hr_set, pt_bosque, sk_snk, sr_set, sv_talbanken, zh_gsd, zh_gsdsimp), 4x NVIDIA A100-80GB GPUs
abstract: Named-entity recognition (NER) in low-resource languages is usually tackled by finetuning very large multilingual LMs, an option that is often infeasible in memory- or latency-constrained settings. We ask whether small decoder LMs can be pretrained so that they adapt quickly and transfer zero-shot to languages unseen during pretraining. To this end we replace part of the autoregressive objective with first-order model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML). Tagalog and Cebuano are typologically similar yet structurally different in their actor/non-actor voice systems, and hence serve as a challenging test-bed. Across four model sizes (11 M – 570 M) MAML lifts zero-shot micro-F1 by 2–6 pp under head-only tuning and 1–3 pp after full tuning, while cutting convergence time by up to 8%. Gains are largest for single-token person entities that co-occur with Tagalog case particles *si*/*ni*, highlighting the importance of surface anchors.

title: Batayan: A Filipino NLP benchmark for evaluating Large Language Models
venue: Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL 2025)
role_in_thesis: Evaluates model performance across authentic Tagalog and code-switched Taglish text to measure linguistic capabilities without translationese bias.
problem: Filipino remains under-represented in multilingual benchmarks, while existing corpora suffer from unnatural translationese and narrow task diversity because they rely on machine translations.
proposed_solution: The authors create Batayan, an eight-task Filipino benchmark curated and validated by native speakers to evaluate understanding, reasoning, and generation across large language models.
claim: Models with dedicated Filipino instruction tuning achieve superior performance across diverse tasks on Batayan, rivaling and occasionally exceeding larger commercial models.
dataset_testbed: Batayan (newly created Filipino benchmark with 3,800 test instances), PAWS, Belebele (Tagalog subset), PH election-related tweets dataset (Cabasag et al., 2019), Balanced COPA, XNLI, XL-Sum, FLORES 200
abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities on widely benchmarked high-resource languages. However, linguistic nuances of under-resourced languages remain unexplored. We introduce Batayan, a holistic Filipino benchmark that systematically evaluates LLMs across three key natural language processing (NLP) competencies: understanding, reasoning, and generation. Batayan consolidates eight tasks, three of which have not existed prior for Filipino corpora, covering both Tagalog and code-switched Taglish utterances. Our rigorous, native-speaker-driven adaptation and validation processes ensures fluency and authenticity to the complex morphological and syntactic structures of Filipino, alleviating the pervasive translationese bias in existing Filipino corpora. We report empirical results on a variety of open-source and commercial LLMs, highlighting significant performance gaps that signal the under-representation of Filipino in pre-training corpora, the unique hurdles in modeling Filipino’s rich morphology and construction, and the importance of explicit Filipino language support. Moreover, we discuss the practical challenges encountered in dataset construction and propose principled solutions for building culturally and linguistically-faithful resources in under-represented languages. We also provide a public evaluation suite as a clear foundation for iterative, community-driven progress in Filipino NLP.

title: Developing a Named Entity Recognition Dataset for Tagalog
venue: Proceedings of the First Workshop for Southeast Asian Language Processing (SEALP 2023)
role_in_thesis: Introduces the gold-standard TLUnified-NER dataset necessary for training and evaluating location extraction in Philippine emergency texts.
problem: Tagalog lacks reliable named entity recognition resources because existing datasets contain noisy silver-standard annotations, narrow domain labels, or restricted access.
proposed_solution: The author created TLUnified-NER, a publicly available gold-standard dataset of 7.8k news documents annotated across three entity types by native speakers, and provided baseline benchmarks.
claim: TLUnified-NER provides a high-quality gold-standard Tagalog dataset where context-sensitive transformer models achieve over 90 F1 and outperform models trained on noisy silver annotations.
dataset_testbed: TLUnified-NER (new gold-standard dataset curated and annotated by the authors), TLUnified pretraining corpus (source of news texts), WikiANN Tagalog portion (reannotated test set used for cross-dataset comparison)
abstract: We present the development of a Named Entity Recognition (NER) dataset for Tagalog. This corpus helps fill the resource gap present in Philippine languages today, where NER resources are scarce. The texts were obtained from a pretraining corpora containing news reports, and were labeled by native speakers in an iterative fashion. The resulting dataset contains ∼\sim7.8k documents across three entity types: Person, Organization, and Location. The inter-annotator agreement, as measured by Cohen’s κ\kappa, is 0.81. We also conducted extensive empirical evaluation of state-of-the-art methods across supervised and transfer learning settings. Finally, we released the data and processing code publicly to inspire future work on Tagalog NLP.

title: calamanCy: A Tagalog Natural Language Processing Toolkit
venue: NLP-OSS Workshop (EMNLP 2023)
role_in_thesis: Provides a unified pipeline architecture for simultaneous sequence labeling and syntactic parsing in Tagalog on constrained computational resources.
problem: Tagalog is a low-resource language whose corpora, treebanks, and language models are scattered, and no unified framework exists for building its NLP pipelines.
proposed_solution: The authors built calamanCy, an open-source toolkit on top of spaCy that provides ready-to-use multitask pipelines for POS tagging, dependency parsing, and named entity recognition in Tagalog.
claim: CalamanCy pipelines are competitive on core Tagalog NLP tasks with a smaller compute footprint, and users with low compute budgets can match multilingual language models using the static vector models.
dataset_testbed: TLUnified pretraining corpus, TLUnified-NER (annotated NER corpus created in this paper), Merged Universal Dependencies treebanks (TRG and Ugnayan), Hatespeech election tweets dataset (10k tweets), Dengue tweets dataset (4k tweets), 64 vCPU machine with 256 GB RAM for pretraining, T4 or V100 GPU for transformer pipelines
abstract: We introduce calamanCy, an open-source toolkit for constructing natural language processing (NLP) pipelines for Tagalog. It is built on top of spaCy, enabling easy experimentation and integration with other frameworks. calamanCy addresses the development gap by providing a consistent API for building NLP applications and offering general-purpose multitask models with out-of-the-box support for dependency parsing, parts-of-speech (POS) tagging, and named entity recognition (NER). calamanCy aims to accelerate the progress of Tagalog NLP by consolidating disjointed resources in a unified framework. The calamanCy toolkit is available on GitHub: https://github.com/ljvmiranda921/calamanCy

title: Language Model Tokenizers Introduce Unfairness Between Languages
venue: 37th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2023)
role_in_thesis: Demonstrates that subword tokenizers cause excessive sequence fragmentation and latency penalties on non-English text during local inference.
problem: Language model tokenizers encode the same content into vastly different numbers of tokens depending on the language, so users of some languages face higher costs, longer latency, and less usable context length for identical services.
proposed_solution: The authors introduce a tokenizer parity measure (the tokenization premium of equivalent sentences across languages, computed on a parallel corpus) and argue that future language models should be trained from scratch with multilingually fair subword tokenizers built on UTF-8 that cover all Unicode codepoints.
claim: No examined tokenizer, including multilingual and byte-level ones, achieves parity across languages: the ChatGPT/GPT-4 tokenizer needs up to 15 times more tokens for the same content in some languages than in English, multilingual tokenizers vary by up to a factor of 13, and byte-level models differ by more than 4 times, so the authors call for multilingually fair tokenizers.
dataset_testbed: FLORES-200 parallel corpus
abstract: Recent language models have shown impressive multilingual performance, even when not explicitly trained for it. Despite this, there are concerns about the quality of their outputs across different languages. In this paper, we show how disparity in the treatment of different languages arises at the tokenization stage, well before a model is even invoked. The same text translated into different languages can have drastically different tokenization lengths, with differences up to 15 times in some cases. These disparities persist even for tokenizers that are intentionally trained for multilingual support. Character-level and byte-level models also exhibit over 4 times the difference in the encoding length for some language pairs. This induces unfair treatment for some language communities in regard to the cost of accessing commercial language services, the processing time and latency, as well as the amount of content that can be provided as context to the models. Therefore, we make the case that we should train future language models using multilingually fair subword tokenizers.

title: The Decades Progress on Code-Switching Research in NLP: A Systematic Survey on Trends and Challenges
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2023
role_in_thesis: Documents methodological trends in code-switching research while highlighting the scarcity of open benchmarks for underrepresented code-switched languages.
problem: Code-switching research in NLP has grown rapidly across many languages, tasks, and methods over recent decades, but the field has lacked a comprehensive systematic survey that consolidates this progress and identifies open challenges.
proposed_solution: The authors conduct the first large-scale systematic survey by collecting and manually annotating more than 400 code-switching papers from the ACL Anthology and ISCA proceedings, categorizing them by languages, venues, paper types, datasets, methods, and tasks, and analyzing how linguistic theories and machine learning approaches have evolved.
claim: The survey finds that neural methods and pre-trained multilingual models have increasingly dominated code-switching NLP while rule-based and statistical approaches decline, that research is heavily skewed toward a few language pairs such as Spanish-English and Hindi-English, and that more than 60% of code-switching datasets remain private, hindering reproducibility.
dataset_testbed: N/A
abstract: Code-Switching, a common phenomenon in written text and conversation, has been studied over decades by the natural language processing (NLP) research community. Initially, code-switching is intensively explored by leveraging linguistic theories and, currently, more machine-learning oriented approaches to develop models. We introduce a comprehensive systematic survey on code-switching research in natural language processing to understand the progress of the past decades and conceptualize the challenges and tasks on the code-switching topic. Finally, we summarize the trends and findings and conclude with a discussion for future direction and open questions for further investigation.

title: Improving Large-scale Language Models and Resources for Filipino
venue: Proceedings of the 13th Conference on Language Resources and Evaluation (LREC 2022)
algorithm_or_model: RoBERTa (Base and Large) pretrained on TLUnified
role_in_thesis: Provides the foundational TLUnified pretraining corpus and monolingual RoBERTa models that serve as the primary Philippine language model baselines.
problem: Filipino, a low-resource language, lacks pretraining corpora and pretrained models that are large and topically varied enough to build robust NLP systems.
proposed_solution: The authors construct TLUnified, a large and topically varied Filipino pretraining corpus assembled from multiple sources with filtering and deduplication, and use it to pretrain RoBERTa Base and Large models that are finetuned on three Filipino classification benchmarks.
claim: Pretraining RoBERTa on TLUnified yields substantial test accuracy gains of roughly four to five points over prior Filipino pretrained transformers across three classification benchmarks.
dataset_testbed: TLUnified (new Filipino pretraining corpus built from OSCAR, NewsPH, and multiple bilingual bitexts), Filipino Hatespeech Dataset, Filipino Dengue Dataset, NewsPH-NLI Medium (regenerated benchmark split), 8x NVIDIA Tesla P100 GPU server
abstract: In this paper, we improve on existing language resources for the low-resource Filipino language in two ways. First, we outline the construction of the TLUnified dataset, a large-scale pretraining corpus that serves as an improvement over smaller existing pretraining datasets for the language in terms of scale and topic variety. Second, we pretrain new Transformer language models following the RoBERTa pretraining technique to supplant existing models trained with small corpora. Our new RoBERTa models show significant improvements over existing Filipino models in three benchmark datasets with an average gain of 4.47% test accuracy across the three classification tasks of varying difficulty.

title: TweetTaglish: A Dataset for Investigating Tagalog-English Code-Switching
venue: Proceedings of the 13th Conference on Language Resources and Evaluation (LREC 2022)
algorithm_or_model: Dictionary-based word-level language identification and regression benchmark models
role_in_thesis: Contributes a large corpus of Tagalog-English social media posts annotated with language distributions to analyze code-switching behavior.
problem: Tagalog and Tagalog-English code-switched text are underrepresented in NLP because Tagalog data is scarce and standard models struggle with mixed-language inputs.
proposed_solution: The authors create TweetTaglish, a dataset of 21,150 code-switched tweets annotated with language distribution percentages using dictionary lookup and validated through regression experiments.
claim: Benchmarking experiments demonstrate dataset validity, with a multilayer perceptron regression model predicting language distributions and outperforming the mean baseline across English, Tagalog, and Other classes.
dataset_testbed: TweetTaglish (21,150 Tagalog-English code-switched tweets)
abstract: Deploying recent natural language processing innovations to low-resource settings allows for state-of-the-art research findings and applications to be accessed across cultural and linguistic borders. One low-resource setting of increasing interest is _codeswitching_ , the phenomenon of combining, swapping, or alternating the use of two or more languages in continuous dialogue. In this paper, we introduce a large dataset (20k+ instances) to facilitate investigation of Tagalog-English code-switching, which has become a popular mode of discourse in Philippine culture. Tagalog is an Austronesian language and former official language of the Philippines spoken by over 23 million people worldwide, but it and Tagalog-English are under-represented in NLP research and practice. We describe our methods for data collection, as well as our labeling procedures. We analyze our resulting dataset, and finally conclude by providing results from a proof-of-concept regression task to establish dataset validity, achieving a strong performance benchmark (R<sup>2</sup> =0.797–0.909; RMSE=0.068–0.057).

title: When is Multi-task Learning Beneficial for Low-Resource Noisy Code-switched User-generated Algerian Texts?
venue: Proceedings of the LREC 2020 – 4th Workshop on Computational Approaches to Code Switching
algorithm_or_model: Multi-task neural network with shared CNN encoders and task-specific decoders
role_in_thesis: Evaluates multi-task learning across sequence labeling and text classification on noisy code-switched social media text.
problem: It is unclear whether multi-task learning benefits low-resource NLP, especially given the scarcity of labelled data for noisy user-generated Algerian Arabic.
proposed_solution: The authors jointly train four Algerian NLP tasks with shared encoders while testing task combinations, task order, word context, data size, and data augmentation.
claim: Multi-task learning helps low-resource Algerian NLP only in specific configurations where task pairing, task order, and training data size determine performance gains.
dataset_testbed: Algerian code-switch detection dataset (Adouane and Dobnik, 2017), Algerian spelling normalisation and correction dataset (Adouane et al., 2019), Algerian sentiment analysis dataset (Adouane et al., 2020), New Algerian code-switched NER dataset created by the authors (46,710 comments, 17,133 named entities)
abstract: We investigate when is it beneficial to simultaneously learn representations for several tasks, in low-resource settings. For this, we work with noisy user-generated texts in Algerian, a low-resource non-standardised Arabic variety. That is, to mitigate the problem of the data scarcity, we experiment with jointly learning progressively 4 tasks, namely code-switch detection, named entity recognition, spell normalisation and correction, and identifying users’ sentiments. The selection of these tasks is motivated by the lack of labelled data for automatic morpho-syntactic or semantic sequence-tagging tasks for Algerian, in contrast to the case of much multi-task learning for NLP. Our empirical results show that multi-task learning is beneficial for some tasks in particular settings, and that the effect of each task on another, the order of the tasks, and the size of the training data of the task with more data do matter. Moreover, the data augmentation that we performed with no external resources has been shown to be beneficial for certain tasks.

title: Comparing the Level of Code-Switching in Corpora
venue: Proceedings of the 10th Conference on Language Resources and Evaluation (LREC 2016)
role_in_thesis: Supplies the corpus-level Code-Mixing Index used to quantify the degree of code-switching across the language profiles of the evaluation data.
problem: Social media made large code-switched corpora available for research, but existing corpus comparison measures assume monolingual text and cannot compare the level of code-switching between corpora.
proposed_solution: The paper extends an earlier utterance-level Code-Mixing Index into a revised utterance measure and a corpus-level complexity score combining matrix language fraction, code alternation points, and switching frequency.
claim: The measure objectively ranks code-switching levels across six corpora and identifies the English-Nepali EMNLP 2014 corpus as the most code-switched with a Cc value of 49.06.
dataset_testbed: Dutch-Turkish online chat corpus (DU-TR), English-Hindi Twitter and Facebook chat corpus (EN-HI), EMNLP 2014 shared task English-Spanish corpus (EN-ES), EMNLP 2014 shared task English-Mandarin Chinese corpus (EN-ZH), EMNLP 2014 shared task English-Nepali corpus (EN-NE), EMNLP 2014 shared task Standard Arabic and Egyptian Arabic corpus (ARB-ARZ)
abstract: Social media texts are often fairly informal and conversational, and when produced by bilinguals tend to be written in several different languages simultaneously, in the same way as conversational speech. The recent availability of large social media corpora has thus also made large-scale code-switched resources available for research. The paper addresses the issues of evaluation and comparison these new corpora entail, by defining an objective measure of corpus level complexity of code-switched texts. It is also shown how this formal measure can be used in practice, by applying it to several code-switched corpora.

title: A survey of joint intent detection and slot-filling models in natural language understanding
venue: ACM Computing Surveys
role_in_thesis: Provides the canonical natural language processing precedent for jointly modeling token-level entity extraction and sequence-level classification tasks.
problem: Although joint models for intent detection and slot filling have rapidly proliferated in natural language understanding, the field lacked an up-to-date, systematic synthesis of the approaches pursued, the issues encountered, the datasets used, and the evaluation practices across this line of research.
proposed_solution: The authors compile and organise the natural language understanding literature up to mid-2020, reviewing intent detection, slot filling, and the joint task along the dimensions of feature engineering, model architectures, addressed issues, datasets, and evaluation metrics, and summarising reported benchmark performance to expose trends and future directions.
claim: The survey finds that joint intent and slot models have effectively saturated the standard ATIS and SNIPS benchmarks, with intent accuracy above 99% and slot F1 around 98%, so the field should shift toward new, more natural datasets, unannotated or few-shot settings, generalisation to new domains, and standardised experimental setups.
dataset_testbed: ATIS, SNIPS
abstract: Intent classification and slot filling are two critical tasks for natural language understanding. Traditionally the two tasks have been deemed to proceed independently. However, more recently, joint models for intent classification and slot filling have achieved state-of-the-art performance, and have proved that there exists a strong relationship between the two tasks. This article is a compilation of past work in natural language understanding, especially joint intent classification and slot filling. We observe three milestones in this research so far: Intent detection to identify the speaker’s intention, slot filling to label each word token in the speech/text, and finally, joint intent classification and slot filling tasks. In this article, we describe trends, approaches, issues, data sets, evaluation metrics in intent classification and slot filling. We also discuss representative performance values, describe shared tasks, and provide pointers to future work, as given in prior works. To interpret the state-of-the-art trends, we provide multiple tables that describe and summarise past research along different dimensions, including the types of features, base approaches, and dataset domain used.

title: Reporting Score Distributions Makes a Difference: Performance Study of LSTM-networks for Sequence Tagging
venue: Proceedings of the 2017 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
role_in_thesis: Evaluates models across multiple random seeds to prevent false conclusions caused by score variation and stochastic optimization noise in sequence models.
problem: Comparing single performance scores for neural networks causes false conclusions because different random seeds make models converge to distinct local minima that generalize differently.
proposed_solution: The authors propose comparing score distributions across multiple runs with different random seeds and evaluating network design choices across thousands of configurations.
claim: Comparing score distributions prevents false conclusions caused by random seed variations and identifies LSTM configurations that improve performance and stability across sequence tagging tasks.
dataset_testbed: Penn Treebank (reduced to 500 training sentences), CoNLL 2000, CoNLL 2003, ACE 2005, TempEval3
abstract: In this paper†† This paper is published in the proceedings of EMNLP 2017. we show that reporting a single performance score is insufficient to compare non-deterministic approaches. We demonstrate for common sequence tagging tasks that the seed value for the random number generator can result in statistically significant (p<10−4p<10^{-4}) differences for state-of-the-art systems. For two recent systems for NER, we observe an absolute difference of one percentage point F1F\_{1}-score depending on the selected seed value, making these systems perceived either as state-of-the-art or mediocre. Instead of publishing and reporting single performance scores, we propose to compare score distributions based on multiple executions. Based on the evaluation of 50.000 LSTM-networks for five sequence tagging tasks, we present network architectures that produce both superior performance as well as are more stable with respect to the remaining hyperparameters. The full experimental results are published in [Reimers and Gurevych (2017)](#bib.bib30 "").11 1 [https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.06799](https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.06799 "") The implementation of our network is publicly available.22 2 [https://github.com/UKPLab/emnlp2017-bilstm-cnn-crf](https://github.com/UKPLab/emnlp2017-bilstm-cnn-crf "")

title: A Design Science Research Methodology for Information Systems Research
venue: Journal of Management Information Systems
algorithm_or_model: Design Science Research Methodology (DSRM) process model
role_in_thesis: Structures the development and offline local deployment of the prototype web application as an operational demonstration artifact.
problem: Although design science was established as a legitimate information systems research paradigm in the early 1990s, it saw little adoption because the field lacked a commonly accepted methodology and a shared mental model for conducting, presenting, and evaluating such research.
proposed_solution: The authors develop the Design Science Research Methodology (DSRM), a nominal six-step process model of problem identification and motivation, definition of solution objectives, design and development, demonstration, evaluation, and communication, together with a mental model for structuring research outputs, and demonstrate it on four published projects.
claim: The DSRM satisfies its three design objectives of consistency with prior literature, provision of a nominal process, and provision of a mental model, and its application to four case studies shows that published design science research in IS fits the methodology, which could aid its acceptance in the discipline.
dataset_testbed: Case study of the CATCH data warehouse for community health assessment (Berndt et al., Miami-Dade County, Florida), Case study of a software reuse measure developed at MBA Technologies (Rothenberger and Hershauer), Case study of the SIP-based CGUsipClient voice- and video-over-IP application for Internet2 (Chatterjee et al., Claremont Graduate University), Case study of the critical success chains (CSC) IS planning method at Digia Ltd. (Peffers et al.)
abstract: The paper motivates, presents, demonstrates in use, and evaluates a methodology for conducting design science (DS) research in information systems (IS). DS is of importance in a discipline oriented to the creation of successful artifacts. Several researchers have pioneered DS research in IS, yet over the past 15 years, little DS research has been done within the discipline. The lack of a methodology to serve as a commonly accepted framework for DS research and of a template for its presentation may have contributed to its slow adoption. The design science research methodology (DSRM) presented here incorporates principles, practices, and procedures required to carry out such research and meets three objectives: it is consistent with prior literature, it provides a nominal process model for doing DS research, and it provides a mental model for presenting and evaluating DS research in IS. The DS process includes six steps: problem identification and motivation, definition of the objectives for a solution, design and development, demonstration, evaluation, and communication. We demonstrate and evaluate the methodology by presenting four case studies in terms of the DSRM, including cases that present the design of a database to support health assessment methods, a software reuse measure, an Internet video telephony application, and an IS planning method. The designed methodology effectively satisfies the three objectives and has the potential to help aid the acceptance of DS research in the IS discipline.

title: Statistical Comparisons of Classifiers over Multiple Data Sets
venue: Journal of Machine Learning Research
algorithm_or_model: Wilcoxon signed-ranks test and Friedman test with post-hoc procedures (Nemenyi, Bonferroni-Dunn, Holm, Hochberg, Hommel)
role_in_thesis: Adopts non-parametric Friedman and post-hoc testing to compare multi-task optimization algorithms across leave-one-event-out disaster splits without normality assumptions.
problem: Machine learning studies frequently need to compare several classifiers over multiple data sets, yet no statistically sound, established procedure exists for this task, so researchers rely on ad hoc methods that either lack statistical grounding or misuse statistical tests.
proposed_solution: The authors review current practice and, based on theoretical and empirical analysis, recommend simple, safe, and robust non-parametric tests: the Wilcoxon signed-ranks test for comparing two classifiers and the Friedman test with its corresponding post-hoc tests for comparing more classifiers over multiple data sets, with results visualized using newly introduced critical difference (CD) diagrams.
claim: The authors conclude that non-parametric tests, namely the Wilcoxon signed-ranks test for two classifiers and the Friedman test with post-hoc tests for multiple classifiers, are safer and empirically at least as strong as parametric alternatives such as the paired t-test and ANOVA, and should therefore be preferred for comparing classifiers over multiple data sets.
dataset_testbed: 14 UCI data sets with binary class attribute (C4.5 AUC worked examples), 40 real-world data sets with discrete classes from the UCI Machine Learning Repository (empirical comparison of tests), ICML proceedings papers from 1999-2003 (analysis of statistical testing practice)
abstract: While methods for comparing two learning algorithms on a single data set have been scrutinized for quite some time already, the issue of statistical tests for comparisons of more algorithms on multiple data sets, which is even more essential to typical machine learning studies, has been all but ignored. This article reviews the current practice and then theoretically and empirically examines several suitable tests. Based on that, we recommend a set of simple, yet safe and robust non-parametric tests for statistical comparisons of classifiers: the Wilcoxon signed ranks test for comparison of two classifiers and the Friedman test with the corresponding post-hoc tests for comparison of more classifiers over multiple data sets. Results of the latter can also be neatly presented with the newly introduced CD (critical difference) diagrams.

title: A Model of Inductive Bias Learning
venue: Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research
algorithm_or_model: bias learning (learning to learn) model, instantiated as neural-network feature learning trained by gradient descent
role_in_thesis: Proves that joint hard parameter sharing across related tasks reduces per-task sample complexity when learning representations from a shared environment.
problem: Standard supervised learning models take the learner's inductive bias (hypothesis space) as given, yet choosing a bias that both contains a solution and generalizes reliably normally depends on hand-crafted expert knowledge, and no formal model explains how such bias could itself be learned.
proposed_solution: The authors formalize a bias-learning model in which the learner, embedded in an environment of related tasks governed by a distribution over tasks, samples multiple tasks and selects a hypothesis space from a given family by minimizing average empirical error, with sample-complexity bounds proving when the chosen bias transfers to novel tasks from the same environment.
claim: The paper proves that a hypothesis space performing well on sufficiently many training tasks from an environment will, with high probability, contain good solutions to novel tasks from that environment, and for neural-network feature learning the examples required per task decay as O(k + W/n) toward the minimum O(k) as the number of tasks grows, with at most O(W) tasks needed for the learned features to generalize.
dataset_testbed: N/A
abstract: A major problem in machine learning is that of inductive bias: how to choose a learner’s hypothesis space so that it is large enough to contain a solution to the problem being learnt, yet small enough to ensure reliable generalization from reasonably-sized training sets. Typically such bias is supplied by hand through the skill and insights of experts. In this paper a model for _automatically learning_ bias is investigated. The central assumption of the model is that the learner is embedded within an _environment_ of related learning tasks. Within such an environment the learner can sample from multiple tasks, and hence it can search for a hypothesis space that contains good solutions to many of the problems in the environment. Under certain restrictions on the set of all hypothesis spaces available to the learner, we show that a hypothesis space that performs well on a sufficiently large number of training tasks will also perform well when learning novel tasks in the same environment. Explicit bounds are also derived demonstrating that learning multiple tasks within an environment of related tasks can potentially give much better generalization than learning a single task.

title: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding
venue: arXiv
role_in_thesis: Provides the bidirectional encoder architecture that crisis classification systems fine-tune, including shared encoders in multi-task triage models and domain-adaptive crisis language models.
problem: Pre-trained language representations relied on unidirectional language models, and this unidirectionality restricted pre-training architectures and harmed downstream tasks that need context from both directions.
proposed_solution: The authors pre-train a bidirectional Transformer using masked language modeling and next sentence prediction objectives, then fine-tune all parameters with one task-specific output layer.
claim: Pre-training a deep bidirectional Transformer with masked language modeling and next sentence prediction achieved new state-of-the-art results on eleven NLP tasks and outperformed task-specific architectures after simple fine-tuning.
dataset_testbed: BooksCorpus (800M words), English Wikipedia (2,500M words), GLUE benchmark (MNLI, QQP, QNLI, SST-2, CoLA, STS-B, MRPC, RTE, WNLI), SQuAD v1.1, SQuAD v2.0, TriviaQA (augmentation data for SQuAD v1.1), SWAG, CoNLL-2003 Named Entity Recognition, Cloud TPU
abstract:
We introduce a new language representation model called BERT, which stands for Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers. Unlike recent language representation models [Peters et al. (2018a)](#bib.bib36 ""); [Radford et al. (2018)](#bib.bib38 ""), BERT is designed to pre-train deep bidirectional representations from unlabeled text by jointly conditioning on both left and right context in all layers. As a result, the pre-trained BERT model can be fine-tuned with just one additional output layer to create state-of-the-art models for a wide range of tasks, such as question answering and language inference, without substantial task-specific architecture modifications.
BERT is conceptually simple and empirically powerful. It obtains new state-of-the-art results on eleven natural language processing tasks, including pushing the GLUE score to 80.5% (7.7% point absolute improvement), MultiNLI accuracy to 86.7% (4.6% absolute improvement), SQuAD v1.1 question answering Test F1 to 93.2 (1.5 point absolute improvement) and SQuAD v2.0 Test F1 to 83.1 (5.1 point absolute improvement).

title: DistilBERT, a distilled version of BERT: smaller, faster, cheaper and lighter
venue: arXiv
role_in_thesis: Shows that distillation retains most encoder accuracy at lower parameter counts and faster inference, supporting the deployment constraints of operational disaster response.
problem: Growing parameter counts in pre-trained language models inflate computational and memory costs, hindering deployment on edge devices and under constrained operational budgets.
proposed_solution: The authors pre-train a smaller general-purpose model, DistilBERT, from a BERT teacher with a triple loss that combines masked language modeling, distillation, and cosine-distance objectives.
claim: Knowledge distillation during pre-training produces a 40% smaller and 60% faster general-purpose model that retains 97% of BERT's language understanding performance and supports on-device use.
dataset_testbed: English Wikipedia and Toronto Book Corpus (pre-training corpus), GLUE benchmark, IMDb, SQuAD v1.1, 8 16GB V100 GPUs (pre-training), Intel Xeon E5-2690 v3 CPU (inference timing), iPhone 7 Plus (on-device inference)
abstract: As Transfer Learning from large-scale pre-trained models becomes more prevalent in Natural Language Processing (NLP), operating these large models in on-the-edge and/or under constrained computational training or inference budgets remains challenging. In this work, we propose a method to pre-train a smaller general-purpose language representation model, called DistilBERT, which can then be fine-tuned with good performances on a wide range of tasks like its larger counterparts. While most prior work investigated the use of distillation for building task-specific models, we leverage knowledge distillation during the pre-training phase and show that it is possible to reduce the size of a BERT model by 40%, while retaining 97% of its language understanding capabilities and being 60% faster. To leverage the inductive biases learned by larger models during pre-training, we introduce a triple loss combining language modeling, distillation and cosine-distance losses. Our smaller, faster and lighter model is cheaper to pre-train and we demonstrate its capabilities for on-device computations in a proof-of-concept experiment and a comparative on-device study.

title: Unsupervised Cross-lingual Representation Learning at Scale
venue: arXiv
role_in_thesis: Establishes the scaled multilingual pretraining baseline for cross-lingual transfer to low-resource languages, including Philippine languages, across classification and entity recognition evaluations.
problem: Multilingual language models pretrain on Wikipedia, which gives limited data, especially for low-resource languages, and the trade-offs of scaling such models to many languages remain poorly understood.
proposed_solution: The authors pretrain a large Transformer masked language model named XLM-R on cleaned CommonCrawl data in 100 languages while evaluating capacity, sampling, and vocabulary trade-offs.
claim: XLM-R sets a new state of the art on XNLI, NER, and MLQA, and shows that a single multilingual model can match strong monolingual models without losing per-language performance.
dataset_testbed: CC-100 (2.5 TB filtered CommonCrawl corpus in 100 languages, created by the authors), Wikipedia corpora (used in ablations and monolingual BERT baselines), XNLI, CoNLL-2002, CoNLL-2003, MLQA, SQuAD (English training set), GLUE, 500 Nvidia V100 GPUs with 32 GB memory
abstract: This paper shows that pretraining multilingual language models at scale leads to significant performance gains for a wide range of cross-lingual transfer tasks. We train a Transformer-based masked language model on one hundred languages, using more than two terabytes of filtered CommonCrawl data. Our model, dubbed XLM-R, significantly outperforms multilingual BERT (mBERT) on a variety of cross-lingual benchmarks, including +14.6% average accuracy on XNLI, +13% average F1 score on MLQA, and +2.4% F1 score on NER. XLM-R performs particularly well on low-resource languages, improving 15.7% in XNLI accuracy for Swahili and 11.4% for Urdu over previous XLM models. We also present a detailed empirical analysis of the key factors that are required to achieve these gains, including the trade-offs between (1) positive transfer and capacity dilution and (2) the performance of high and low resource languages at scale. Finally, we show, for the first time, the possibility of multilingual modeling without sacrificing per-language performance; XLM-R is very competitive with strong monolingual models on the GLUE and XNLI benchmarks. We will make our code, data and models publicly available.

title: Rethinking embedding coupling in pre-trained language models
venue: arXiv
role_in_thesis: Shows that decoupling input and output embeddings reallocates parameters toward deeper layers and improves multilingual transfer at identical fine-tuning parameter counts.
problem: Tying input and output embeddings forces both matrices to share one dimensionality, which pushes multilingual models to spend a large share of their parameter budget on input embeddings.
proposed_solution: The authors decouple input and output embedding shapes, shrink input embeddings, enlarge pre-training output embeddings, and reinvest saved parameters into wider or deeper Transformer layers.
claim: Reallocating parameters away from input embeddings improves performance at identical fine-tuning parameter counts, allowing RemBERT to outperform XLM-R on XTREME despite using 3.5 times fewer pre-training tokens.
dataset_testbed: XTREME benchmark tasks: XNLI, PAWS-X, Wikiann NER, XQuAD, MLQA, TyDiQA-GoldP, Wikipedia dumps in 104 languages for mBERT-scale pre-training, Wikipedia and Common Crawl text in 110 languages for RemBERT pre-training, MNLI, SQuAD, Word embedding association test datasets: MEN, MTurk771, Rare-Word, SimLex999, Verb-143, WMT16 English-German sentence pairs for nearest-neighbor translation, NLP probing tasks from Tenney et al. (2019), Google Cloud TPUs (64 for pre-training, 8 for fine-tuning)
abstract: We re-evaluate the standard practice of sharing weights between input and output embeddings in state-of-the-art pre-trained language models. We show that decoupled embeddings provide increased modeling flexibility, allowing us to significantly improve the efficiency of parameter allocation in the input embedding of multilingual models. By reallocating the input embedding parameters in the Transformer layers, we achieve dramatically better performance on standard natural language understanding tasks with the same number of parameters during fine-tuning. We also show that allocating additional capacity to the output embedding provides benefits to the model that persist through the fine-tuning stage even though the output embedding is discarded after pre-training. Our analysis shows that larger output embeddings prevent the model’s last layers from overspecializing to the pre-training task and encourage Transformer representations to be more general and more transferable to other tasks and languages. Harnessing these findings, we are able to train models that achieve strong performance on the xtreme benchmark without increasing the number of parameters at the fine-tuning stage.

title: Canine: Pre-training an Efficient Tokenization-Free Encoder for Language Representation
venue: Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics
role_in_thesis: Removes subword vocabulary requirements through character-level encoding, addressing segmentation brittleness that affects code-switched and low-resource text.
problem: Explicit tokenization with fixed subword vocabularies is brittle across languages and restricts how well pretrained encoders can represent and adapt to diverse text.
proposed_solution: The authors propose Canine, a tokenization-free encoder that embeds raw Unicode characters with hash embeddings and downsamples the sequence with strided convolutions before its deep transformer stack.
claim: A tokenization-free character encoder with downsampling outperforms a comparable mBert on multilingual question answering while using fewer parameters, and with vocabulary-free n-grams it stays competitive on named entity recognition.
dataset_testbed: TyDi QA (multilingual question answering, 11 languages), CoNLL 2002 and CoNLL 2003 named entity recognition data (Spanish, Dutch, English, German), MasakhaNER (ten African languages), multilingual Wikipedia corpus of mBert (104 languages) for pre-training, 64 Cloud TPUs v3
abstract: Pipelined NLP systems have largely been superseded by end-to-end neural modeling, yet nearly all commonly-used models still require an explicit tokenization step. While recent tokenization approaches based on data-derived subword lexicons are less brittle than manually engineered tokenizers, these techniques are not equally suited to all languages, and the use of any fixed vocabulary may limit a model’s ability to adapt. In this paper, we present Canine, a neural encoder that operates directly on character sequences—without explicit tokenization or vocabulary—and a pre-training strategy that operates either directly on characters or optionally uses subwords as a soft inductive bias. To use its finer-grained input effectively and efficiently, Canine combines downsampling, which reduces the input sequence length, with a deep transformer stack, which encodes context. Canine outperforms a comparable mBert model by 5.7 F1 on TyDi QA, a challenging multilingual benchmark, despite having fewer model parameters.

title: TwHIN-BERT: A Socially-Enriched Pre-trained Language Model for Multilingual Tweet Representations at Twitter
venue: Proceedings of the 29th ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining
role_in_thesis: Demonstrates that social engagement signals improve multilingual tweet representations, supporting domain-adaptive pretraining for short and noisy social media text in crisis settings.
problem: Most pre-trained language models target general text corpora, so they handle short, noisy user-generated text on social media poorly and ignore the social engagement signals inside social networks.
proposed_solution: TwHIN-BERT is a multilingual Twitter language model pre-trained with masked language modeling plus a contrastive social objective built from socially similar Tweet pairs mined through network embedding.
claim: TwHIN-BERT outperforms established multilingual and Twitter-specific language models on both social engagement prediction and semantic classification tasks, and the social objective produces the largest gains on social tasks.
dataset_testbed: 7 billion Tweets in 100 languages collected from Jan. 2020 to Jun. 2022 for pre-training, with 100 billion user-Tweet engagement records covering 1 billion Tweets, Twitter Heterogeneous Information Network (TwHIN) with about 200 million users, 1 billion Tweets, and over 100 billion engagement edges, Curated Tweet engagement prediction dataset sampled from the 50 most popular languages on Twitter, Curated multilingual Tweet hashtag prediction dataset covering 50 popular languages, SemEval2017 Task 4A English sentiment dataset, SemEval2018 Task 2 emoji prediction datasets in English and Spanish, SemEval2020 Task 9 code-mixed sentiment datasets in Hindi+English and Spanish+English, ASAD Arabic Tweet sentiment dataset, COVID-JA Japanese Tweet topic classification dataset, 16 Nvidia A100 GPUs (a2-megagpu-16g) and a FAISS index on a 16 A100 GPU node for training and pair mining
abstract: Pre-trained language models (PLMs) are fundamental for natural language processing applications. Most existing PLMs are not tailored to the noisy user-generated text on social media, and the pre-training does not factor in the valuable social engagement logs available in a social network. We present TwHIN-BERT, a multilingual language model productionized at Twitter, trained on in-domain data from the popular social network. TwHIN-BERT differs from prior pre-trained language models as it is trained with not only text-based self-supervision but also with a social objective based on the rich social engagements within a Twitter heterogeneous information network (TwHIN). Our model is trained on 77 billion tweets covering over 100100 distinct languages, providing a valuable representation to model short, noisy, user-generated text. We evaluate our model on various multilingual social recommendation and semantic understanding tasks and demonstrate significant metric improvement over established pre-trained language models. We open-source TwHIN-BERT and our curated hashtag prediction and social engagement benchmark datasets to the research community1.

title: XLM-V: Overcoming the Vocabulary Bottleneck in Multilingual Masked Language Models
venue: arXiv
role_in_thesis: Shows that a one-million-token vocabulary overcomes the shared vocabulary bottleneck that reduces token coverage for low-resource languages in multilingual encoders.
problem: Multilingual language models keep a vocabulary near 250,000 tokens even as parameter counts grow, and this fixed size limits token coverage and representation quality across more than 100 languages.
proposed_solution: The authors build a one million token vocabulary by clustering lexically similar languages, allocating vocabulary capacity per cluster, and pretraining a masked language model named XLM-V with this vocabulary.
claim: A one million token vocabulary lets XLM-V outperform XLM-R on every tested multilingual understanding task, with the largest gains on low-resource languages.
dataset_testbed: CC100, MultiNLI, SQuAD v1.1, XNLI, MLQA, XQuAD, TyDiQA-GoldP, WikiAnn (PAN-X), Americas NLI, MasakhaNER, FLoRes-200, 256 NVIDIA A100 GPUs
abstract: Large multilingual language models typically rely on a single vocabulary shared across 100+ languages. As these models have increased in parameter count and depth, vocabulary size has remained largely unchanged. This vocabulary bottleneck limits the representational capabilities of multilingual models like XLM-R. In this paper, we introduce a new approach for scaling to very large multilingual vocabularies by de-emphasizing token sharing between languages with little lexical overlap and assigning vocabulary capacity to achieve sufficient coverage for each individual language. Tokenizations using our vocabulary are typically more semantically meaningful and shorter compared to XLM-R. Leveraging this improved vocabulary, we train XLM-V, a multilingual language model with a one million token vocabulary. XLM-V outperforms XLM-R on every task we tested on ranging from natural language inference (XNLI), question answering (MLQA, XQuAD, TyDiQA), to named entity recognition (WikiAnn). XLM-V is particularly effective on low-resource language tasks and outperforms XLM-R by 11.2% and 5.8% absolute on MasakhaNER and Americas NLI, respectively.

title: mmBERT: A Modern Multilingual Encoder with Annealed Language Learning
venue: arXiv
role_in_thesis: Demonstrates that modern encoder architecture and annealed language learning extend multilingual pretraining to more than 1700 low-resource languages under a modest compute budget.
problem: Recent encoder-only language model research has largely ignored multilinguality, so the six-year-old XLM-R model remains the strongest multilingual encoder for classification and retrieval tasks.
proposed_solution: The authors pre-train mmBERT, a ModernBERT-style encoder, and progressively add languages while lowering the masking rate, holding over 1700 low-resource languages until the short decay phase.
claim: mmBERT outperforms previous multilingual encoders on classification and retrieval, while decay-phase training on low-resource languages matches or exceeds large models like o3 and Gemini 2.5 Pro.
dataset_testbed: FineWeb2 (pre-training corpus), FineWeb2-HQ (pre-training corpus), MegaWika v2 (pre-training corpus), Dolma (pre-training corpus), Dolmino (mid-training corpus), GLUE, XTREME, MTEB (MMTEB v2, English and multilingual), CoIR, MS MARCO (embedding fine-tuning), XNLI, PAWS-X, TiQuaD, FoQA, NVIDIA H100 and L40S GPUs
abstract: Encoder-only languages models are frequently used for a variety of standard machine learning tasks, including classification and retrieval. However, there has been a lack of recent research for encoder models, especially with respect to multilingual models. We introduce mmBERT, an encoder-only language model pretrained on 3T tokens of multilingual text in over 1800 languages. To build mmBERT we introduce several novel elements, including an inverse mask ratio schedule and an inverse temperature sampling ratio. We add over 1700 low-resource languages to the data mix only during the decay phase, showing that it boosts performance dramatically and maximizes the gains from the relatively small amount of training data. Despite only including these low-resource languages in the short decay phase we achieve similar classification performance to models like OpenAI’s o3 and Google’s Gemini 2.5 Pro. Overall, we show that mmBERT significantly outperforms the previous generation of models on classification and retrieval tasks – on both high and low-resource languages.

title: SEA-LION-ModernBERT and Embedding
venue: Hugging Face
role_in_thesis: Defines the regional encoder backbone candidate for Taglish disaster triage, combining Southeast Asian language coverage with efficient ModernBERT architecture and tokenizer fertility gains.
problem: Complex regional scripts and diverse Southeast Asian languages suffer from high tokenization fertility and poor representation in standard encoder models.
proposed_solution: The authors combine ModernBERT with a Gemma 3 SentencePiece tokenizer and train encoder models on three trillion tokens across 13 regional languages.
claim: Adopting the Gemma 3 tokenizer with ModernBERT improves tokenization fertility and computational efficiency for cross-lingual tasks across Southeast Asian languages.
dataset_testbed: 2T pre-training token corpus (code and 13 Southeast Asian and regional languages), 1T mid-training token corpus (code and 13 Southeast Asian and regional languages), 245 million EN-EN and EN-SEA text pairs for contrastive pre-training (600M variant), 8 million multilingual text pairs for fine-tuning (600M variant), SEA-BED (Southeast Asia Embedding Benchmark, 169 datasets across 10 SEA languages), CMTEB (Chinese Massive Text Embedding Benchmark), MTEB (Massive Text Embedding Benchmark), Nvidia H200 140GB GPUs (SMC H200 cloud infrastructure)
abstract:
SEA-LION is a collection of Large Language Models (LLMs) which have been pretrained and fine-tuned for the Southeast Asia (SEA) region.

This encoder-only model leverages the advanced ModernBERT architecture combined with the Gemma 3 SentencePiece tokenizer. The adoption of the Gemma 3 tokenizer with ModernBERT allows the model to achieve highly efficient and culturally nuanced text processing. This combination significantly improves the tokenization fertility and compression rates for complex regional scripts and diverse Southeast Asian languages, enabling the model to handle longer context windows and cross-lingual tasks with greater computational efficiency.

To achieve this level of performance, the model was developed through a rigorous, multi-stage training pipeline. The foundation was established through extensive pre-training on 2 Trillion (2T) tokens, followed by a mid-training phase on an additional 1 Trillion (1T) tokens. Both of these massive training phases comprehensively covered code alongside 13 specific languages: Burmese, Chinese, English, Filipino, Indonesian, Javanese, Khmer, Lao, Malay, Sundanese, Tamil, Thai, and Vietnamese.

title: Decoupled Weight Decay Regularization
venue: International Conference on Learning Representations
role_in_thesis: Supplies the AdamW optimizer whose decoupled weight decay underpins the optimizer-controlled comparison conditions of the proposed benchmark.
problem: L2 regularization and weight decay regularization are equivalent for standard stochastic gradient descent but not for adaptive gradient methods, which confounds regularization comparisons in deep learning.
proposed_solution: The authors decouple the weight decay term from the gradient-based optimization step of Adam, producing the AdamW update rule.
claim: Decoupled weight decay improves generalization over L2-regularized Adam, and its optimal value is more independent of the learning rate schedule.
dataset_testbed: CIFAR-10 image classification with ResNet, WMT English-German machine translation with Transformer models, Language modeling with recurrent and self-attention networks
abstract: The authors show that L2 regularization and weight decay regularization are not equivalent for adaptive gradient methods such as Adam, because the adaptive rescaling couples the decay term to the gradient statistics. They propose AdamW, a variant that decouples weight decay from the gradient-based optimization step. Experiments on image classification, language modeling, and machine translation show that decoupled weight decay yields better generalization than L2 regularization and that its optimal value interacts less strongly with the learning rate schedule.
